review_text_clean: this site is used to take money from tourists. it is that simple. 4500rs for an adult foreigner to enter. on arrival at the museum to buy your ticket you will be surrounded by local tour guides trying to be employed. they do not take no for an answer. ignore them walk the site yourself. they will tell you it is too big to be walked, trust me, it does not require a tuk-tuk. walk. the museum was worth one trip round, but better to get to the ruins themselves. once there, they are lovely to see. amazing history. all of which can be walked around. the temple to the north was really special and well kept. it is the local tack sellers and temple life guards blowing their whistles which ruined the day for me. they walk around in shoes whilst barking at tourists to remove theirs - its ridiculous - especially given how hot the sand is in the sun. its all a money making scheme, which is such a shame. worth the trip, but be stern with the vulture-like salesmen and take lots of water on a hot day.

review_text_clean: we visited polonnaruwa on a typically hot, humid day, which wouldve been no big deal except for the fact that we did a tour of their museum too. i mean, knowing its hot and humid, i can accept that it will be tiring under the sun while viewing the ancient ruins. but i really, really thought it was downright pathetic of them to call their museum a museum, because thats indoors, and it was a literal oven cooking everyone inside alive. we visited the museum prior to actually viewing the ruins, and there, the ventilation is not poor, its non-existent. its so damn stuffy you have difficulties breathing, and while there are these industrial air-conditioners fixed from the wall, they are not in use at all. instead, they put fans and those coolers around, expecting these little machines to provide the ventilation and cool air the place actually needs. it was an epic fail. unless you stood right in front of a cooler, youd feel like youre burning from inside out, all the time. the moment you step way from a fan or a cooler, the heat literally engulfs you. the museum content is actually quite interesting. the ruins themselves were also impressive. but the ventilation and air-conditioning of the museum is worse than crap. if i could i would just visit the ruins and skip the oven they call their museum.
aspect_sentences: ['its so damn stuffy you have difficulties breathing, and while there are these industrial air-conditioners fixed from the wall, they are not in use at all.', 'the moment you step way from a fan or a cooler, the heat literally engulfs you.']

review_text_clean: spent half a day exploring the ruins of polonnaruwa and very much enjoyed this unesco world heritage site. it was a hot day and wed thought about cycling around, but ended up having our taxi driver take us around. the sites are quite spread out, so its definitely worth having transport to get around. bring a pair of socks for the sites that require shoes to be removed e.g. at the vatadage. must sees within the compound, if you are short on time, are the gal vahara for buddha statues and vatadage. personally found the lankatilaka viharaya of most interest - its a large site and there was hardly anyone there - it was a very atmospheric as a result. polonnaruwa is a fascinating site which cant be missed if in the area. try come early before it gets too hot and the big tour groups. food and snacks are readily available around the site.
aspect_sentences: ['food and snacks are readily available around the site.']

review_text_clean: we have to be honest we did not know much about this ancient site before our visit, as we were with a large tour group and just tagged along. this was once the capital of sril lanka or ceylon in those days. its now a unesco world heritage site. certainly interesting and sometimes referred to as the angkor wat of sri lanka. we wouldnt go quite that far, but the day was dragging on a bit and we didnt visit all the possible sites within. we did a down a dirty visit for about 3 hours, being shuttled to each sitesight, it was a really hoy day and the ground was cooking, the shoes off rule when visiting scared sites was a challenge, so we werent keen to hang around. eight hundred years ago this was the place to be, now just ruins are left of its former glory, we hit the high points as directed by our guide. the quadrangle - a concentration of important monuments ie, temple of the tooth of buddha. rankoth vehara dagoba - a massive stupor, at 54 metres high and gal vihara - beautiful rock carvings, buddha, and some others as we were with a group the tickets were just part of the package, however, the entrance fee for foreigners is 4500 lkr or 25 usd, seems a bit much, as independent travellers we might have thought twice.
aspect_sentences: ['we did a down a dirty visit for about 3 hours, being shuttled to each sitesight, it was a really hoy day and the ground was cooking, the shoes off rule when visiting scared sites was a challenge, so we werent keen to hang around.']

review_text_clean: the former medieval capital city of polonnaruwa covers a very large area and you need to allow several hours to walk around the many temple ruins and statues. it is arguably the most important archaeological site in sri lanka that is still being discovered today. it is no wonder its a unesco site. at times you will need to remove your shoes to enter some off the temples. beware that their are plenty of mischievous monkeys here that may charge at you if you get too close and please do not feed them. you will also experience many locals trying to sell you postcard, wood or other souvenirs. i thoroughly recommend this site to visit and it sits comfortably as a major attraction with nearby sigiriya rock fortress lions rock.

review_text_clean: this is a fascinating place to wander around for a few hours. but these ancient ruins are spread over a vast area, so youll need a car to get around. we were told it takes around 3 days to see it all not that you need to but our trailfinders guide showed us the highlights in a morning. a lot of it is quite similar and can easily be skipped. sections of it are impressive to say the least and some of it less so. my girlfriend thought parts of it reminded her of angkor watt. this is a religious site so make sure you cover shoulders and knees, this isnt just a suggestion. we saw one lady having a right tantrum when they refused to let her in one of the temples, because she wasnt dressed appropriately. even when another member of the public offered to lend her a scarf she carried on screaming at the guards, which had no effect whatsoever. also make sure you dont pose for photos with your back to budda, its a big no no. there are monkeys everywhere, so avoid carrying food or drink and theyll totally ignore you. we saw what happens if you have food and its not pleasant. pollonaruwa ruins are impressive, intriguing and well worth seeing. it was definitely one of my highlights of our sri lanka trip. iain, london
aspect_sentences: ['there are monkeys everywhere, so avoid carrying food or drink and theyll totally ignore you.', 'we saw what happens if you have food and its not pleasant.']

review_text_clean: this is one of the ancient capitals of sri lanka, centuries old and with a number of sites contained therein. entry is usd 25 for foreigners and usd 12.5 for children half rate for nationals of saarc countries. payment can be made in usd or lkr, but change is returned in lkr only. paying in usd is every so slightly cheaper when you do the reverse forex rate calculations. upon paying the entry fee, you can enter the area and see all the various attractions. there is not a lot of information available on-site, so hiring a guide can be worthwhile. there is a museum in the building where you buy tickets, entry to which is complimentary with the polonnaruwa tickets. however if running short of time, can skip this which is what we did. since there are around 26 sites within the premises all spread apart, it can easily take upwards of 1 whole day to see the place in its entirety and enjoy its beauty. if running short of time, you need to plan in advance and shortlist the places you want to see and first finish those and then, time permitting see as much of the rest as possible. the golden quadrangle, palace complex and gul vihara are some of the places that i would recommend as must-see. suggest carrying a lot of water, wearing hats and covering knees. as with most historic ruins, children and people without a sense of history will find this dull, so i would suggest they opt out instead of paying 25 usd and then realising that they didnt appreciate the beauty of the ruins.

review_text_clean: we were pleased we hired bikes - from polo at the cafeteria in the museum car park - to explore this interesting site. a relatively quick trip around the museum allowed us to orientate ourselves as well as get an idea how the site originally looked before we set off along the main road before taking the turn into the site itself. we immediately headed north and enjoyed the less crowded gal vihara - awe inspiring- and monastery area before joining the crowds at the quadrangle and royal palace group. the latter was rather disappointing- we had previously strolled around the free entry island park group of ruins near the museum and found them to be more informative and certainly more comfortable. allow 3-4 hours - on bikes - to explore the main site and be prepared to observe standard temple visit practices - remove shoes, hats and cover shoulders and knees - at multiple stages of the visit. water very welcome although there are multiple vendors en route. we visited in august - sri lankan school holidays and ahead of the apparently imminent rainy season - so many parts of the site were crowded. an early start might be wise.
aspect_sentences: ['water very welcome although there are multiple vendors en route.']

review_text_clean: approximately 25 to get in but worth every last cent. unlike places such as angkor wat, polunnaruwas sites are all completely different making for a stunning day out. ideally, do it over two days. we crammed all the top sites into one day and it was exhausting. we were staying in sigiriya and negotiated a lkr5000 fee with our tuk tuk driver to pick us up from the hotel, take us to all the main sights and then drop us off back at the hotel. a great deal, considering it was a round trip of about 6 hours. you need to dress appropriately for polunnaruwa. knees and shoulders covered. and theres a lot of shoes off. good tip to wear ankle socks as the bare stones do heat up as the day goes on. we saw a lot of people biking the ruins, but theres no overstating just how hot it gets out here, so i wouldnt recommend it. youre better off in a tuk tuk. enjoy!

review_text_clean: the world heritage ruins at polonnaruwa appear to be on the list of every tour that passes through sri lankas cultural triangle. we were staying locally so could get a head start on most of the tours before they poured in. most people seem to cycle around the ruins and i could see why this would be attractive - its cheap, easy and safe, and you can move between the different sites fairly quickly. however, we were advised by a local to head to the top of the site by tuktuk then walk back to town, and id highly recommend this approach too - youll get to see a lot more wildlife when youre walking, and trust me theres a lot to see if you keep your eyes open! saying that, youll probably be fairly tired by the end, and make sure you take plenty of water. the ruins comprise of a number of main sites interspersed by smaller, less-visited sites. be prepared for crowds at the main sites, with far fewer tourists at the smaller ones. all are worth a visit though. ok, this is not angkor or bagan, so dont expect it to be - ive been to both those and still reckon this is worth a visit if youre up in the cultural triangle. however, i wouldnt bother staying in polonnaruwa, id probably stay somewhere else - such as dambulla - and get a tuktuk across for the day.
aspect_sentences: ['be prepared for crowds at the main sites, with far fewer tourists at the smaller ones.']

review_text_clean: once an ancient capital of sri lanka, polonnaruwa is a must-see on any visit to this beautiful island. the site itself is vast, with lots of ruins of ancient stupas, temples, water gardens, monks lodgings, moats, etc dotted around. it must have looked somewhat like angkor wat in its heyday. it is also hauntingly beautiful now, and although one of the more popular tourist sites, never seems crowded because of its vast size. towards the end of the site are exceptional and magnificent representations of the buddha carved in stone - standing, seated and laying down. definitely not to be missed!... for me however, the most intriguing building of all at this ancient site is a very odd and out- of- place i.e.not buddhist nor hindu temple that has puzzled even eminent archaeologists which bears remarkable similarity to the architecture of the pyramids of the ancient maya. how can that be possible?...... a real mystery!
aspect_sentences: ['towards the end of the site are exceptional and magnificent representations of the buddha carved in stone - standing, seated and laying down.']

review_text_clean: keep in mind that the ticket office and the entrance are not in the same place! the tickets are a bit pricey, 4000 rupees per person aprox 25 us per person. where the ticket office is, is also the small museum where you can read about the site. dont forget to take a map from the ticket office it is free! no way of getting around otherwise. it is a huge place, and my advice is to hire a tuk tuk to drive you around from one ruin to another. i think it is the best way to explore this amazing ancient site! we hired a tuktuk from sigiriya to take us to polonnaruwa and around polonnaruwa. it took us 145 minutes to get there from sigiriya, and we spent another 2-3 hours exploring the ruins of the site with a tuktuk, walking would take us the whole day. that half a day trip with a tuktuk cost us 5000 rupees. use your bargaining skills i saw you can hire a bike to explore around the ruins, but considering the sun above us, not the best option if you want this option, take some hats and sun protection most places there you will have to take you shoes off, so if your feet cannot handle heat, bring socks with you! the sand and the stone can get really hot. also, like all buddhist holy places, keep you shoulders covered and wear longer pants. there are a lot of vendors there where you can buy cold drinks, but a bit exspensive. i think it is a nice trip for families, couples, friends - everyone. you can buy nice suvenirs there like wooden elephants and buddhas. but remember, always bargain! we bought a small wooden carved elephant- the original price was 4500 rupees, and we bought it for 1000 rupees. walking away after not agreeing on the price is the best method

review_text_clean: we hired bikes and biked around. first get your tickets at the museum down by the canal and then walk up to the main entrance and hire bikes right outside. they are pretty old but its mainly all flat. entry usd25 and they were happy to take usd. go early as it gets hot looking around. biking helped with a breeze and places to purchase drinks along the way. do your homework prior to your visit and have an understanding of the ruins. also helps with knowing where you want to go. so we went in the entrance gate and looked at the ruins to the right. then went to the far end gal vihara etc and worked our way back. they checked our tickets in a couple of places so keep tickets handy. also remember to bring something to cover up and easy to remove shoes. socks were required on the hot stones. its definitely achievable in a half to 34 day depending upon how interested you are.

review_text_clean: we thoroughly enjoyed our visit here, and the ruins are amazing. our favourites were the image house next to the freshly painted white stupa, and the temple with four huge carved buddhas including the reclining one. some tips to make your visit more enjoyable are- if you have a driver, use them to take you around the site. there is a lot of walking at each of the sites anyway, but it is so spread out that it is not possible to see everything, and even with the bicycles available for hire it would be exhausting just getting between the various ruins. make a priority list of what you want to see as you cant do it all. there is very little information available at each of the ruins, so take a guidebook or print out information from the internet before you go. make sure to wear clothes that cover the shoulders and knees or you wont be allowed to enter some parts. wear shoes that are easy to get on and off as you will need to do that continuously. take old socks to wear as the rocks can be very hot. use plenty of sunscreen and take a hat and water as it can be very hot indeed. enjoy - an amazing place.

review_text_clean: the ruins are really impressive and only really need a day. the most impressive are gal vihara or rock monastery and lankatilaka. we went in the afternoonearly evening and so this meant it was much cooler and probably slightly more enjoyable. we decided to go by tuk-tuk and our driver tried to make us go with his special price. this entailed not buying the official ticket and paying him the cash instead which he could use to bribe the guards. overall he tried to convince us this would save us approximately rs 2000. we felt really uneasy about this and declined, deciding to buy an official ticket. he then got really angry and then refused to drive us to the north site. we spoke to a local about this and apparently it is a really common scam and those that have gone with the bribery option havent been able to get in to see some sites, particularly gal vihara. our advice would be to be very clear before getting in the tuk-tuk about what is going to happen.

review_text_clean: came here for the day with my partner and our three youngest. our guide drove us between each site but there was still a lot of walking and it was very hot - so make sure you take plenty of water and a parasolumberella for children to shade themselves whilst we were there we saw 2 local children faint due to the heat. there is plenty to see and the ruins and architecture provide plenty of photo opportunities - although there was some confusion as to what you could include in your photos - we knew from visiting other areas that you must not take selfies or pictures that show you or your party with your backs to any buddas, however our guide who was a local sri lankan told us that if you stood next to a budda - ie at its side and not with your back to it then that was fine. however when we did this we were told off and made to delete the photos - our guide did not understand this and spoke to the man who made us delete the photos at some length and told us that this had never been an issue before - however, best advice is do not have any people in your photos wherever they are standing!! in addition, please dress respectfully. also, there are parts where you must remove your shoes so we always carried a little pair of socks with us when visiting any of these type of places so we could pop them on as the ground was not only stony but extremely hot! we saw a lot of people who simply had to miss out some of the areas as they could not walk on the ground in bare feet due to the heat.

review_text_clean: the polonnaruwa site is as magnificent as the reviews say it is and it is a must do on your sri lanka trip. dont just do the big name buildings, royal palace, quadrangle and gal vihara though. take the time to stroll through the huge monastery ruins between the quadrangle and gal vihara and make sure you check out lankathilaka. make a detour too to see the only frescoes remaining on the whole site at the tivanka image house in the far north. the only small downside of our day was right at the beginning when we went to the museum to buy our tickets. the tickets were lkr 7950 for two. we paid with 2 x lkr 5000 notes. the tickets were handed over with an lkr 1000 note and a lkr 50 note. i waited. the ticket lady put her hand in the drawer and pulled out a stack of lkr 100 bills and started talking to me. as the conversation continued, she put her hand and the notes back in the drawer. chat over, there was a pause.you have to give me more money, i said. she pulled her hand out of the drawer, counted out some lkr 100 bills and pushed them over. i picked them up. there were nine. one more please, i said. she peeled one more off and laid it down. not a word. i counted everything out again, said thank you and walked away, making a mental note to include this in my review to warn future travellers. thats it. its still a terrific place to visit, just watch out for the short-changers at the ticket office.
aspect_sentences: ['make a detour too to see the only frescoes remaining on the whole site at the tivanka image house in the far north.']

review_text_clean: we stayed at sigiri and travelled out each day to polonnurawa and anuradhaphura. polonnurawa is certainly worth a visit. there is really a lot of history here. we came with a tour guide so we got the low down on the history. again expect to pay for the admission which is around 3500 lkr pls check before going each. this is about the same price as for anuradhaphura . the majority of the entrance fees go towards maintaining the site and further excavations, so you are funding a good cause. after paying for the admission do go round the museum which is where you get the admission tickets. the visit to the museum is worthwhile especially if you dont have a guide. it explains each monument and the history behind it. and also the history as to why the kings moved from anuradhaphura to polonnurawa to start a second kingdom. all the places are concentrated in one small area so walking from one to another is quite straightforward. polonnurawa started in the 10th century as the capital city and ended around the 12th century . apparently it had lain undiscovered until british archeologists began probing in the late 19th century when the whole area was covered in forests. when you look at the buildings do look at the surrounding trees. their bases are about 1.5 m to 2 m above the ground of the excavations. it will have taken some serious excavations to get to the monuments. some places are just spectacular. the royal palace for one, the second is the lake or a tank as they call it. this huge lake of 25 sq km was manually excavated in the 12th century by people and elephants. it really is quite an awesome task. there are some temples which are in ruins and previously held the scared relic of the tooth now housed in kandy. just do note that the dress code applies to temple ruins as to living temples. no shorts, or crop tops and no slippers on the temple grounds even abandoned ones. a few visitors were caught out and not allowed in. having visited both polonnurawa and anuradhaphura i think if you dont have enough time then polonnurawa is the better choice. but if you have the time and inclination then do visit both places .
aspect_sentences: ['this is about the same price as for anuradhaphura .']

review_text_clean: we visited this site in early february on a fairly warm day i.e. temperature about 23 degrees. we had guide with us. the advantage of a guide is that they can help you make the most of your visit by selecting out what to see and more importantly they have the knowledge of what is inter-connected and in close proximity too. this is massive heritage site and you cannot explore all of it in one day so selecting out points of interest and finding them is a challenge. best to read up about it before you arrive as that may help you select out what you think suits you best. alternatively just meander and explore. there is an option to hire cycles and that could be a good way to explore the site. whether walking or cycling or with a driver guide you will almost certainly come across structures which will amaze you. the architecture is a delight if you have not previously seen buddhist or hindu heritage sites before. one of the joys was seeing carved granite carvings in the structures which convey stories. hindu architecture is very different from buddhist architecture. one revers the buddha without much reference to the animal kingdom and the other is prolific in carving animals, grotesque masks and moonstones with story telling symbolisms threaded throughout the buildings and statues. one is also relatively simplistic in design while the other is over complicated, yet they are in harmony too. so this a site where you can marvel at the size and shapes of early structures, whether they be structures like a giant wedding cake or stupas which are round and dome like. another joy of visiting this place is the sense of freedom you have to explore it. however there is an obligation that visitors show extra respect for those sites with a special religious significance. this presents no problems if your address is appropriate i.e. no knees men and women showing and the female head is covered. however this applies only to certain special places here not all of them. this is also a site that has grass and avenues of trees to contrast with the massive brick structures. until i visited this place i never realised that bricks were being made in the 12 century and were being used to build multi storey buildings and places of worship. if you are not keen on heritage ruins and history you will probable not rate these sites very much. for me it was interesting, enjoyable, varied and wonderful because of it heritage. i have not previously seen a nothing quite like it on this scale despite travelling to over 20 countries.
aspect_sentences: ['the advantage of a guide is that they can help you make the most of your visit by selecting out what to see and more importantly they have the knowledge of what is inter-connected and in close proximity too.']

review_text_clean: this is a must do on any trip up into the cultural quarter of sri lanka. this is a uneso world heritage site which in its hey day was in the 11th12th century and was one of the most important cities in sri lanka.overall it is not bad shape! there is so much to see that you should plan on spending 12 a day here. you can walk it but it could be quite exhausting and extremely hot and there are no shops for water etc. hire a bike or better still an ac car. you should hire a guide as they have a wealth of knowledge and it will avoid you missing out on stuff. i suggest that you start in the museum next to where you pay, the head south to potugal hihara, then do the royal palace complex, then the quadrangle and then work you way up the site to gal vihara the star of the whole show then head a tad further north to the lotus pond and finally the tivanka-patamaghara a hidden gem. doing the complex properly makes a great day!
aspect_sentences: ['doing the complex properly makes a great day!']

aspect_sentences: ['practicalities polonnarawu covers a large area, so walking the whole site, which covers a large area, might be a challenge - particularly in the 30 degrees heat.']

review_text_clean: great to learn about the various aspects of ancient history in sri lanka. you can bike, walk, drive a car or hire a tuk tuk. make sure to cover up though as it is roasting out there!! im told by my sri lankan in laws that this part of sri lanka rarely sees rain hence the intense heat. for me the heat started to take away from it a bit cause it was so intense but i did still enjoy the historic side of it and cycling!! cool to see but definitely recommend to go earlier in the day before heat rises too much! also be prepared to take off shoes, hats and have your shoulders and knees covered to be able to enter and walk around the amazing temples whose infrastructure have remained largely preserved. recommend. three stars only because of the heat and humidity which i know cant be helped.

review_text_clean: we really enjoyed this archeological site and spent a good few hours here. its very impressive. its in the jungle there are lots of monkeys, so dont bring food inside. we hired a motorcycle from sigiriya, from wew thawulla restaurant, and saw all the sites via motorcycle. because the site is very big, some people hire a bicycle to see the place. you can also go by tuk tuk. some drivers will try to get you to pay all fees to them, instead of the paying the park entrance fee, but know that if you do this, the money does not go towards the park for restorations, so please make the right decision and pay the entrance fee to help the conservation and maintenance for this beautiful site. you can park at the entrances, but when you enter each area, you must take off your shoesyou will be taking them off a lot. from sigiriya, its a one hour drive. costs 30 to enter site. ticket office is not at the entrance, its around the corner.

review_text_clean: polonnaruwa was the thriving commercial and religious centre of sri lanka some 800 years ago. it consists of a lot of temples and religious buildings. it is unecso world heritage site. before we went into the ruins of the ancient city, we visited the archaeological museum next to the ticket office. i am recommending this museum for all of tourists, after that no need for a tourist guide in to the ancient city you will recognize all main buildings and tourist sites from the photos and stories in the museum. you can walk, rent a bike or go by car depends of your time and interesting. the enter ticket price is 25person and you can pay with us dollars. the best time to visit polonnaruwa is in the morning, to avoid high temperatures and hot weather. the opening time is 7am-630pm daily. we spent more then 4 hours there and we really had a nice time. after touring we took a lunch in the lake house, which is so nice place for a rest. built in 1870 as a circuit bungalow for british government agents, the old polonnaruwa rest house and once the queen of englands holiday destination in the 1960s, has now been restored and renamed as ekho lake house. go and enjoy on this amazing place!

review_text_clean: we visited the site today independently. to enter you must first purchase your ticket through the museum 50 us which also entitles you entry to the museum. the entry to the site is about a kilometre away, you can traverse the site by a number of options - walk, bicycle or tuk-tuk. you can hire a guide to explain all of the different areas for a price if you like. because of the distances around the site we chose to use a tuk-tuk we negotiated a price with the driver dont pay over 2000 lkr as we wanted him for over 4 hours. you will be overwhelmed by the history dating from the 10th century i believe. most of the structures are in a state of disrepair but it looks as if the government is taking steps to rectify this. you may wear hats and footwear and take photographs in all places except religious shrines and monuments but this is signed to make you aware. be aware this site can get extremely hot but there are plenty of stalls selling cold drinks as well as the usual trinkets, souvenirs,post cards etc. there is a place just past the museum behind the ekho lake house called island park which is free to the public and contains some sites. this world heritage site should not be missed.

review_text_clean: i hired a tuk tuk for 5000r for a return journey from sigiriya including waiting time. the ancient ruins which were abandoned over 700 years ago cover around 4km north to south, and there are about 6 or 7 main sites spread short distances apart from each other, but too far to walk in the baking heat, so having the tuk tuk was ideal. i did however see some people who had hired cycles, but it was too hot for me! it was 4525r entrance fee with the ticket office next to the museum, but there wasnt much to see and the information and presentation was quite dated. fortunately my driver ordered the sites so i started with the smaller less impressive sites first, followed by the more impressive ones late on, including the 55 metre high red brick rankot vihara dagoba and the quadrangle of dalada maluwa which at one point housed the buddha tooth relic. remember many of the sites are holy so you need to remove shoes when entering, so bring socks as walking bare foot on the stones gets hot! also a real no no is taking pictures posing with your back to any buddhas. if youve been to some of the major buddhist archaeological sites like ankor wat, bagan, borobudur etc. you wont be blown away, but still this was very enjoyable, and you can easily spend a day seeing the full city. this was one of my favourite attractions in sri lanka.
aspect_sentences: ['the ancient ruins which were abandoned over 700 years ago cover around 4km north to south, and there are about 6 or 7 main sites spread short distances apart from each other, but too far to walk in the baking heat, so having the tuk tuk was ideal.']

review_text_clean: what is not explained at the museum is where to go and the distances one needs to cover to see all the main ares. the island gardens are just behind the museum at the back of the car park sign says road closed. the more extensive site is over the road and about half a mile away. so basically if you arrive with transport make sure they stay. pay for your tickets 25 head, spend 30 minutes or so at the museum, walk to back of the car park to do first section, then take your transport to the main site and again keep them with you to drive between sites. do not attempt to walk the site, its enormous and in the heat i would not recommend. each site is fascinating but unless you are an architectural boffin, pace yourself and consider reading up before you go and picking areas of particular interest. we spent over 4 hours here and were completely exhausted.

review_text_clean: we stayed in pol in order to see the archaeological ruins. on our arrival day we walked round the small site directly beside ekho lake side hotel where we are staying, this appears to be free of charge and was a useful introduction. the next day we bought a ticket from the main ticket centremuseum and hired a guide. hiring a guide on-the-street as it were is always a gamble, the first person who latched on to me appeared to speak ok english, but after asking him a few questions it was apparent that his english was not really much good. the second person who approached me claimed to have been an english language teacher and was much better - but far from perfect. im not sure that a guide you pick up on the street is really worth the hassle. ours was quite useful in the museum, but his interest waned during the next few hours and having made enough money from me was keen to get back to his family for the rest of poya day. i thought we had agreed a price, his reccollection was slightly different take a piece of paper, write down the agreed price and each kepe a copy! and when it came to tips, it was ok, then he suggested i also give him something for his lunch, then he spotted that my wife had s in her purse and so suggested 10 towards his air fares fund! so altogether cost about double what i thought we had agreed - but at the end of the day wasnt really much in european terms. you would probably be better off with a good guide book and research printed off before you went. the sites are fairly spread out and the entrance is about 2-3kms from the ticket office. so you need transport we already had a van and driver for this part of our trip, i guess that visiting all the central sites and then back to the museum was about 5-10kms, so its not surprising that the further you travel the less busy the sites become - and actually they are the best parts, tivanka image house in particular. some hire cycles to go round the sites - i would not reccomend it in 30 degrees unless you are very fit. i would like to have spent more time there but 3-4 hours seemed to be the expectation of the guide and our driver. if i had wanted to visit for even 30 minutes the next day it would have cost another 50 for two of us. having been to the angkor wat archaeological sites the previous year, there is no comparison, angkor is much larger, much busier, much more interesting but also more expensive, but you can buy 3-day non consecutive tickets.

and when it came to tips, it was ok, then he suggested i also give him something for his lunch, then he spotted that my wife had s in her purse and so suggested 10 towards his air fares fund! so altogether cost about double what i thought we had agreed - but at the end of the day wasnt really much in european terms. you would probably be better off with a good guide book and research printed off before you went. the sites are fairly spread out and the entrance is about 2-3kms from the ticket office. so you need transport we already had a van and driver for this part of our trip, i guess that visiting all the central sites and then back to the museum was about 5-10kms, so its not surprising that the further you travel the less busy the sites become - and actually they are the best parts, tivanka image house in particular. some hire cycles to go round the sites - i would not reccomend it in 30 degrees unless you are very fit. i would like to have spent more time there but 3-4 hours seemed to be the expectation of the guide and our driver. if i had wanted to visit for even 30 minutes the next day it would have cost another 50 for two of us. having been to the angkor wat archaeological sites the previous year, there is no comparison, angkor is much larger, much busier, much more interesting but also more expensive, but you can buy 3-day non consecutive tickets.

review_text_clean: polonnaruwa is a well maintained and well enough run ancient cityarchaeological site in the cultural triangle. its very easy to get around via tuk tuk and fairly inexpensive too or you can go the bike route if you dont mind the heat. there are a number of sites to see but it can all be done in about three hours if you have a tuk tuk. visitors should be prepared for crowds of people, many of whom will ignore well placed and easy to read signs about taking off shoes and not climbing on crumbling walls. there will be people in all of your pictures as well. ultimately i have two different recommendations re whether to visit 1 if you have never seen a similar site i would recommend going - you will be interested the whole way through. 2 if you have been to multiple other sites as i have, including in cambodia, throughout thailand and burma this is ok to skip. i grew bored pretty quickly and didnt see anything newdifferent that made it worth a special trip. if you are in the area with an afternoon to kill as i was there are way worse ways to spend your time but be prepared to be underwhelmed.

review_text_clean: as i was staying in dambulla, i had to take a bus to visit polonnaruwas sights. from the main street of dambulla, there are regular buses heading towards kaduruwela which is an adjacent part of polonnaruwa where the train and bus stations are located. hopping onto any bus that is heading to kaduruwela will get you into polonnaruwa. however, it is best to tell the bus conductor to drop you off in the old town, which is i think the first main drop-off as you enter polonnaruwa from the direction of dambulla. the bus journey took about 90 100 minutes, and cost 100 rupees. after getting off the bus in the old town, ask around to get to the museum -- just short walk away along a canal -- where you can buy a combined ticket for the museum and the archaeological sights. it cost 3975 rupees but is valid only for one day. the museum gives a so-so introduction to the history of the sri lankan kingdoms, putting the ruins of polonnaruwa into a larger context. curation has room for improvement. moreover, the airconditioning was weak and it was warm and humid inside the place. the ticket comes with a pretty useless map. the staff know that the map is useless. so the lady advised me to take a photo of the wall-mounted map which gives clearer directions of where the ruins are situated. whats so difficult about designing and printing a new map? the fact that no one has yet done so gives you a clue about shoddy management standards. from the museums exit, walk northwest through a small garden to the group of ruins on the shore of the lake known as parakramabahu samudera. then walk east and cross the main road, to the entrance to the other section of the ruins. your ticket will be checked again. the ruins are in three main clusters the lakeshore cluster also known as the island group, the royal palace cluster and the quadrangle cluster, each about 500m from each other. but there are plenty more sites scattered a few kilometres around. some ruins are in bad shape the ones in the sacred quadrangle are perhaps in the best condition. it wasnt possible to cover much more than the three main clusters in the time a daytrip that i had. based on my experience, id say that if you want to examine most of the ruins, i think you will need a much earlier start, which means staying in polonnaruwa the night before and the night after. i am rating his site as merely average. even allowing for the fact that ruins that are 800 - 1100 years old cant possibly be in good condition, when i compare it with other archaeological sites of similar vintage around the world, polonnaruwa is not outstanding. the stone construction does not look to have been built to a high standard the sculpture works were relatively few and not particularly good aesthetically. the fundamental reason, i suppose, is that the kingdom over which polonnaruwa controlled was probably a smallish one by world standards and it might never have had the resources to build a truly great capital city. as a second-class city, today we have second-class ruins. add to that sub-par management, lack of cafes and toilets in the sites despite the heat and great distances... and my feeling at the end of the day was a degree of dissatisfaction.

review_text_clean: we spent an enjoyable few hours exploring this ancient site. we were on a bit of a tight time deadline and were torn between polonnaruwa or anuradhapuda, am glad we chose the former as its a fairly compact, self contained site, with good access to all the ruins. yes its not as glamorous as other countries ancient sites, but it is of great historical and cultural significance in sri lanka and several of the buildings are well preserved to say they were buried beneath jungle for centuries! there is ample parking and good visitor facilities toilets, wash facilities, food and drink we travelled around by car, which was straightforward enough. there are several services hiring out push bikes, which seemed a pleasant way of getting around. we had a very informative guide book, which we used to navigate and inform our route round. there are some information boards dotted around, but they dont give particularly detailed descriptions. as with any historic site visit, there are several guides hanging around offering their services, if you are without a guidebook and find a good guide i would recommend it as you will miss out on a lot of information and even miss some of the well hidden sites altogether! you do need to remove headwear and footwear to enter a large number of the sites, so come prepared and maybe bring something to dust the gravel off your feet after. i would highly recommend a visit here during a tour of sri lankas cultural triangle.

review_text_clean: definitely a must-visit if you are in center-north sri lanka. the views from the bottomgarden are already great, but from the top it looks amazing. not recommended for people with vertigo due to the last round of steps or impaired mobility. climbing is easy even for elder people as long as you make a few stops on the way up i went with my father 65 yo, that has some problems doing long walks climbing, but stopping a few times worked out very well for him. managed to go up and down in a total time of 57 minutes. the history of this place is also very interesting. you can get leaflets at entrance. expect lots of locals trying to guide you up i think its totally unnecessary to hire one specially considering the very poor english skills..but its up to you. they will try hard. the only bad thing is families that dont respect the wasp warning signs resulting in incidents. wasps can be triggered by sound - as advertised everywhere. unfortunately we saw families with kids screaming, loud music and others crying out loud precisely in the designated wasp attack zone. avoid going with kids to keep this place safe for everyone or at least take them to non-attack zones.
aspect_sentences: ['the views from the bottomgarden are already great, but from the top it looks amazing.']

review_text_clean: offers lovely views of the region. there are about 600 steps to climb, the first few are steps in rock and later on steel steps bolted on rocks. the climb is steep but doable. contrary to earlier reviews, all the steps now are in perfect condition and it is safe to climb. there are railings throughout so you have something for support. there is a lush green garden before you begin the climb and a small musuem. while on top, you can see the remains of the foundation of the erstwhile palace, and the pond swimming pool. there are only about a few trees so make sure you carry sun protection and plenty water and some snacks. there are no shops shacks en route or on top. on the way down, you can climb up a few stairs again for paintings in the cave. ps if youre from saarc countries, do not forget your passport. the ticket prices are significantly lower for saarc citizens but youll get that rate only if youre carrying the passport, soft copy is not accepted.

review_text_clean: loved our trip here, we went in the morning arriving by 9am and it wasnt too busy at all. the museum part at the start is a bit rubbish of the old photos but it was nice to see the jewellery and things uncovered from the site. the walk along the flat to the rock just brings home the scale of the place its just incredible. the climb up is all even steps and in different sections, the first part is steady wide stone steps with places to stop on the way. once at the top of that you can see the stone lions feet as the entrance of the fortress itself. there are some dogs monkeys about so be careful of having food and drink out here but they were very calm and i never saw them trying to get anything from people. from here its tight metal steps and no places to stop but not as bad as it looks from the bottom. once at the top of the fortress there is beautiful views over sri lanka. easy to spend and hour or so wandering around and some places to sit and enjoy the views too. definitely worth the money. not sure how anyone can moan about the difference for tourists and locals - is their country of course they should enjoy it cheaper and tourists who can afford to travel should pay more to upkeep this beautiful place.
aspect_sentences: ['there are some dogs monkeys about so be careful of having food and drink out here but they were very calm and i never saw them trying to get anything from people.']

review_text_clean: what can i say, this is one of the highlights of my 13 day trip to sri lanka! there are govt approved guides at base if you want to have a little history lesson and guide all the way to the top. i declined because i wanted to experience without alot of talk. obviously i went when tourism was down in sri lanka so there were only about maybe 25 people or so i got to enjoy to myself. i took over a 100 photos and had all developed. there is photo opportunities at every step. the hike up and down took me about 3 hrs but i took my time, its steep but im used to hiking uphill. i can say its safe but i would recommend being fit. the cost as i saw some complaining is not expensive of what you get to see. this is on the same scale as machu picchu or chichennitza in cancun. so ignore those posts. 30is nothing to someone who comes from the west and travels that far!!. on a historical note this fortress dates 500 yrs before christ. theres only one place at the top which you cannot take photos and a man sits there so you dont and thats ancient buddhist frescos which very colorful. once again, this fortress is an incredible place
aspect_sentences: ['30is nothing to someone who comes from the west and travels that far!!.']

review_text_clean: i and my boyfriend are a living proof that this place is manageable even on a rainy day. actually, the experience is amazing! there were almost no people, shorter or none queues. just bring a raincoat or an umbrella, and open sandals, and you will be fine. the complex consists from the rock that you will climb using the famous stairs. in the second half of this journey, there is something called mirror wall and then frescoes, which is a small cave with very old pictures with still vivid colors. the place is full of self-employed tour guides - locals that will follow you around, saying that they are tour guides and that you definitely need one. then they will walk with you, talk with you, and expect money at the end. we were warned that there is no need for a tour guide and that the place is mostly about walking the stairs and the view afterwards. lions paws is the stairway where are normally those long lines of people that are trying to get to the top of the rock. at t the base of the stairs, there are statues in a form of lions paws, so hence the name. this place is what you want to experience when someone talks about sigiriya rock. and form my experience, its the biggest fun! the mirror wall itself is not that wow, i would say. its not shiny anymore, you cant touch it, its just therein its not shiny form. frescoes that are waiting for you at the end of the line are much more interesting, since its something to look at. the line leading to the frescoes is heading among the mirror wall. its not possible to take pictures of frescoes, thought, there is a lot of staff watching everyone so nobody does it. i didnt see any toilets on the way, just those at the ticket office. so count with that, if you want to spend few hours of wondering at the place, or if the queues on the particular day are too long.
aspect_sentences: ['its not possible to take pictures of frescoes, thought, there is a lot of staff watching everyone so nobody does it.']

review_text_clean: beautiful ancient rock fortress! easy climb. we really enjoyed the views. only reason im giving it a 2 starts is because of our guide. we actually had a great time once he left us alone. be careful with tour guides and helpers we had a man following us from the start and he was talking about the sigiriya rock. after approximately 5 minutes he stated that he was a freelance guide and offered to accompany us to the top while telling us about the history of this rock fortress. he stated that he didnt have a price and we could decide at the end what to pay him depending on how we liked his services. we agreed. about 5 minutes after that he brought us to a man selling magic boxes and insisted we try to open them. we were not interested in buying any boxes. a few minutes after that his friend arrived and started helping me up the stairs. i did not ask for help nor was it needed. he insisted on holding onto my hand however it was very awkward and opposite of helpful. it quickly became hazardous as none of the steps are the same size and walking with a stranger like that out of the blue was weird. this helping up the steps became annoying and i tried numerous times to stop it but he kept holding his hand out. my husband was actually walking behind us and thought it was the funniest thing. its funny now looking back at it. he even snapped some photos. after a few more sets of steps i had to tell my husband that i am not climbing 1200 steps and up the rock like this. luckily we were still in the beginning. my husband told our guide who translated to the helper that his assistance was not needed. we were then told he doesnt work for free! our guide then told us that his services were 40-50! we paid less for a taxi drive with all our luggage from the airport to our hotel! be careful! we told both of them to have a nice day however the guide still wanted money for his services thus far ruins the experience!

review_text_clean: my vertigo has got worse with age. it was put to the test getting up the stairs to the top of the rock, but thankfully one of the local guides put his hands on my waist and guided me up. it gave me a little bit of security that i needed to finish the trek. the fact there was one of sri lankas many cute stray dogs at the top of the rock just rubbed salt into the wound and made me realise i should have been a little more robust. sigiriya is one of sri lankas best-known sites to see and it easy to understand. it is an incredible archaeological site, and the mind boggles when you reach the top passing the ancient steps people clambered up, and you realise a whole civilisation lived here. the views from the top are truly breathtaking and well worth the wobbly legs on the way up. monkeys and butterflies and fortunately no hornets were enough distraction from the rocky drop below. the walk-up is a workout, and i was dripping with sweat when i reached the top but having said that it was over 30 degrees, so dripping with sweat was just the norm. if you go to sigiriya and dont think you will make it to the top, then i would recommend not going. getting to the top is what this excursion is about, and once there, the sense of achievement is tremendous but more significant is the experience of what you see all around. there are plenty off guides around if you want one. i would have got one personally, but my partner is a little more frugal and not as free-tipping as i. but when a man is willing to hold the waist of another grown man with wobbly legs to get him to the top - he deserves a tip. sigiriya is the kind of place that now lives in my dreams, and for that, i am grateful.

review_text_clean: i am in my early sixties, with a lung condition. was very hesitant to climb the zillion or so steps, so climbing this was , for me, a trial of resolve. i managed it, but took my time. sri lanka, right now, is sparsely touristed-but not at sigiriya. i would dread to think what it is like when the overseas visitors arrive back en masse, once the memory of the 2019 bombings and coronavirus are ancient history. this place gets crowded and people taking it slow like me tend to get in the way of the more fit individuals. mind you, i was not the slowest by far. unfortunately, however, being slow attracts the attention of helpers. fit young sri lankans standing like hungry carrion, scanning for prey and constantly picking at the perceived weak ones and assisting up each flight of stairs, whether that attention was requested , required or not. their keen eye for a sucker is uncanny and they latch onto a potential monetary catch like seagulls on a chip, regardless of whether you are struggling or not. if you are not quick with a kind hearted rebuke, then they claim their prize and the hassling for large tips starts. they have a hide like an elephant and nothing short of an angry expletive will shake them off. be aware. these guys get aggressive and persistent if you dont make it absolutely clear that you do not wish their assistance. however, you are not out of the woods, as a couple more of these vultures wanting an easy kill will be at the next flight and the process starts again. i hated that and my patience and initial good natured banter was retired in short order. this spoiled things for me, but that is just my personality. being honest, sri lankans are a good natured and, largely, well mannered bunch, but i set my standards for other peoples behaviours at, possibly, unrealistic levels. this is a dirt poor country trying to provide for its peoples and the population have grown to act in a certain way to feed their families. their behaviours are borne from a need to earn money and, as a result, they can be a bit pushy bordering on exasperation at times. did i enjoy the sigiriya experience? well, besides the huffing , puffing and wanting to turn back at every step, i guess i did. was that enjoyment because i was using the climb as a yardstick for my failing fitness and a small mental personal victory was my just reward? probably. would i do it again? - not a chance!
aspect_sentences: ['these guys get aggressive and persistent if you dont make it absolutely clear that you do not wish their assistance.']

review_text_clean: this was our second time of climbing the rock having done it two years ago. amazing place and every step is worth the effort. this attraction is vastly improved from our last visit however there was a few things that could of been clearer. guides now are registered and have to be engaged before you enter the ticket site. they should cost no more than 2000 rupees but some folks where charged 5000. the car parks are different than before and you are dropped off outside the ticket office however your car or tuk tuk then collects you after your climb in the foreigner car park in a different area. no issues as such but this means you must do the museum before you climb. some guides just want you to commence your climb and dont give you this choice. also it is not clear when you buy your ticket. the friends of sigiriya are still at the bottom to assist you up if you require and this can cost 2000 rupees or more. the ticket price is 30 each and when you now exit there is a little market selling what you would expect at variously different prices depending on which one you would chose. the toilets in the foreigner car park are extremely good. this attraction is worth a 5 star review but the lack of information regarding the museum and the car parking arrangements just made it a four.

review_text_clean: an amazing place that you must visit, if youre in sri lanka. most package or guided tours will take you here or get a taxituk-tuk, and if they have any sense, youll arrive early in the morning, that way you not only miss the queues at the entrance, but you can be up, down, and gone before the hot sun makes it even more difficult! there are a lot of steps 1200, and some of them are steephigh, and some of them are a little bit scary - especially if you have a poor head for heights. there are no facilities for wheelchairs. in fact, you probably need be pretty able bodied to do this one. we had a guide who took us slowly from the top to the bottom, stopping to show us the small details we might otherwise have missed, and also to give us a breather! there are plenty of things to see before you reach the upper staircase. but once you are at the top, it provides a spectacular view though early morning mist can limit this, and there are some extensive ruins. youll be scratching your head trying to figure out how they got all the bricks up there. get there early to beat the queues the stairs are very narrow, or get there later for a clear view. take your pick. definitely one of the highlights of my trip to sri lanka. theres nowhere else like it. tips - wear sensible shoes, carry water, and although a hat is useful, it can get pretty windy up the top, so hang on to it.

review_text_clean: quick review to say that this site is not to be missed. but i found no reviews on how vertiginous the climb up might be. clearly it wld be steep climb but for those who have a slight fear of heights the issue is whether you felt safe making the climb. we asked a few of our fellow hotel guests the night before and had a mixed response. so we gave it a try. however i only got one third of the way up via means of a broad staircase which reached a platform with some terrific views over the countryside. but then onwards it became more challenging as i saw a steel caged spiral staircase built into the rock face. i knew straight away i wld freeze half way up and not be able to come down! so i agreed that my partner would carry on up and i would meet him an hour later down in the visitors car park. i had an enjoyable hour watching everyone come and go for an hour and the wonderful vistas knowing i had made the right decision. this was confirmed by my partner when he got back to say it only got worse going up and he witnessed a number of people being vertiginously challenged on the way down. phew! but it sounds worth the challenge if you know you can get back down. i was happy with my own 13 way up kind of achievement! later found out that the steel spiral walkway to see some cave paintingsis not obligatory and can be bypassed as you make your way further up. but you still faced further open and steep staircases built into the rock face. but not me!
aspect_sentences: ['but it sounds worth the challenge if you know you can get back down.']

review_text_clean: well worth a visit. recommend that you take one of the numerous guides who are at the entrance waiting for tourists to roll up. they all wear a uniform polo shirt so you know that they are offical guides, however as like anywhere you need to be prepared to negotiate a price. we paid 20 us for a guide for 3 hours, our guide was excellent giving you a lot of background to the fortress which you would not get from reading the information pamphlet you get given with your ticket. there are toilets located just by the ticket office, very clean but no toilet paper so make sure you take tissues. there is also a water station before you enter with purified drinking water where you can fill up your water bottle. be prepared to climb up narrow stairs to get to the top, the view is amazing and worth the climb. when we went in feb there were no hornets which we had read about however we were told that it was the wrong season. beware of monkeys everywhere which is all part of the sri lankan experience. when you exit the fortress there are numerous toilet blocks which were all clean and well maintained, again take your tissues. make sure you wear comfortable walking clothes, shoes, hat and take water, there is nowhere to purchase water along the way until the exit. we arrived about 9.30ish which we found to be fine, the heat was bearable, the timing of your visit will all be dependent on the time of year you go.

review_text_clean: my husband and i were here 4 weeks ago and decided to go early in the morning at 7am as the heat and humidity was just horrid anyway and thought it would be less then, but it really wasnt. anyway we went shortly after opening time which is at 7am. now, we are both nearly 60 years old and totally unfit fatties and both of us have bad hearts, bad knees and ankles, plus me with an already sprained ankle from a collapsing bridge a week earlier, but hey, i wasnt going to come all this way from australia and not climb this sigiriya rock right?. anyway we climbed to the very top in 50 minutes from the very start to the very top, including a few stops in between to catch our breath and trying to stop out hearts from exploding, but just quietly were were so very proud of ourselves, so kudos to us. now just a word of warning, for those of you who have really bad knees or ankles this climb is not for you, and if you have even the slightest fear of heights, this climb is definitely not for you. id say go as far as the lions feet and thats it as it is really frightening after that especially if people are trying to get past you and your clinging to the edge of the rock for grim death while letting them pass. for those of you who are not scared of heights then go on up to the very top, the 360 degree view you will love and you get to see all the ruins also. i must say watch out for the scammers too who will approach you along the way up at different points, they will make conversation with you and try and help you get up rocks etc and they will start to tell you all about the rock and the history and then they will become your guide without you even knowing about it and it will cost you money, but if you want to use them then go ahead, these locals are desperate for money. also when you get there, there is no signage, well in english anyway, to where you buy the entry tickets from, we found it a bit confusing where to go to get the tickets, and thats a walk in itself too. there are plenty of tuk tuks at the bottom when you come back down that will take you back to your hotels at a reasonable price. just be aware that where the tuk tuks will drop you off at the start where you buy your tickets from is not the same place where you finish up when you come back down from the rock, you seem to get rail roaded out a different exit to an other side of the rock so you end up having to go past all the souvenir stalls. our rooky mistake was telling our tuk tuk driver to pick us up here where he dropped us off, and he failed to tell us this was not the spot you finish up at when you come down from the rock, so once we came down and realised this was not where we started from, we then had to figure out how to get back around to the other side of the rock where the entrance was to meet our tuk tuk driver who was waiting so patiently for us, it was a long walk in the heat. all in all, we were both glad we did it and didnt drop dead from heat exposure and blown heart valves. we never want to see another step again as long as we live, our knees and ankles were aching for days afterwards. but done it now and so a big tick off our bucket list.

review_text_clean: nothing prepared me for this and i was glad i was wearing sturdy trainers. the climb is quite steep for the uninitiated! its a combination of stone steps, some rickety and on occasions nothing to hold onto and metal open stairs, with railings. you really have to look where youre going! there are various stopping points on the way so you dont have to do it in one go. a good tip - our guide took us up early, as it opened - about 7.30 i think. we were at the top by 9. its quite a steep climb in parts and not for the fainthearted, but i didnt see anyone turning back. when you get to the top its a stunning 360 degree vista and well worth the climb. how they ever built a palace up there several hundred years ago, i cant imagine. there are various interesting features on the way up and down, one being the wall paintings, hundreds of years old. you have to climb up a metal spiral staircase on the side of the rock, but you are caged in. as with many things in sri lanka, its very ad hoc! what an amazing morning!
aspect_sentences: ['there are various interesting features on the way up and down, one being the wall paintings, hundreds of years old.']

review_text_clean: we decided to venture to sigiriya rock, to climb to the top in order to see its famous views. on the way to the rock itself, we were surrounded by beautiful manicured grounds, gardens, and pools. as i have a fear of heights, i wasnt sure what to expect. i will say that i struggled on the the way up and going down, as my anxiety took over. my other half had no issues, but i found the narrow and very open stairs difficult to traverse. having to stop a few times, not due to the physical activity, but for me to be able to control my vertigo. the trek, and shaky legs, were worth it as the views were worth it. from the top, you can view a 360 degree view that sri lanka has to offer. one view was reminiscent of a jurassic period of a beautiful lake leading to a distant mountain. you will also see remnants of a fortress, as well as some wildlife mind the cheeky monkeys, as they will steal what they can. i would highly recommend it, as the adrenaline rush is great. those with a paralysing fear of heights... dont go. note go early, bring water and sunscreen, as there is very little shade on the top. also, go to the bathroom before heading up, as there are no facilities on the the way up and on top a poor gentleman learned the hard way ??.
aspect_sentences: ['i would highly recommend it, as the adrenaline rush is great.']

review_text_clean: this is one of the impressive unesco world heritage sites we have visited. steep entrance fee lkr5,460 per person, but it is well worth it! since 5th century, this place was built by the king kashyapa who killed his father, king dhatusena, usurping the throne of his father. he eventually fled to sigiriya from anuradhapura to avoid the retaliation of his half-brother, moggallana who was the rightful heir of the throne. kashyapa ordered to build fortress and palace on top of sigiriya rock. eventually, moggallana came to sigiriya for revenge and war was declared between the brothers. kashyapa lost the battle and committed suicide, and moggallana returned to anuradhapura after winning the battle, and sigiriya rock was converted to a monastery. four parts to appreciate this site first, the fortress at the foot of the rock with viewing site of sirigiya rock from far after passing by the main entrance surrounded by moat. some of the highlights are the summer palace, cobra hood cave, etc. second, the decoration of the authentic fresco half way up to the rock, reachable by spiral staircase. third, the small plateau half way up the rock with massive gateway of lion rock with gigantic rock carvings of lion paw as entrance to the palace to the top of the rock. fourth, where is the last part at top of rock where the ruins of the palace is located. the idea of building a palace on top of a massive rock is already very incredible! 360 degree panoramic views from the top is amazing with sunset view in the evening. in summary, this heritage consists of intriguing historical background, plus the incredible architecture back then in 5th century. it is one of the highlights of our sri lanka trip!
aspect_sentences: ['four parts to appreciate this site first, the fortress at the foot of the rock with viewing site of sirigiya rock from far after passing by the main entrance surrounded by moat.']

review_text_clean: awesome 5th century palace split into 2 sections. one palace is at the bottom of the rock and the other at the top. many many many steps, even on the lower section and they can be uneven and worn in places. a lot of the steps still have their original white marble coverings and when the are wet are extremely slippy. get a guide, the whole history of the place is brought alive. the guides dont have a set cost, you just tip them what you think their service was worth. the frescoes are incredible. i would say that getting here halfway up is a must, even if you cant make it to the top. the rock formations and the construction techniques used to build the place are quite awe inspiring. the views from the top are simply stunning, but it rained the day that we were there and was somewhat misty. you may want think about if the climb is worth it on a rainy day. slight downer was that you had to run the gauntlet of the looky looky men on the way out and the attendants in the free public toilets practically hold you to ransom for toilet paper and a tip. very long journey by private car to get there about 4.5 hrs from the bentota area south of colombo.
aspect_sentences: ['the guides dont have a set cost, you just tip them what you think their service was worth.']

review_text_clean: trip advisor sigiriya i am writing this mainly for people who, like me, have a fear of heights. most reviews focus on the effort of getting up the rock. i am moderately fit and found it hardly taxing at all. my apple watch said i had climbed 48 flights of stairs but it did not feel anywhere near that much. more of a challenge for me was the height and especially the two separate flights of iron stairs. i had debated whether to do the climb at all and was pretty apprehensive. having done it, my advice would be to do it if you have a mild fear of heights or a moderate fear that is under control ie not subject to serious panic attacks. it also helps to have a supportive companion. i would suggest not doing it if your fear is more severe. most stairs are stone with balustrades but there are two iron sections- one that leads up from the mirror wall via a caged-in iron spiral staircase to the cave paintings. you go up to the paintings but then have to come down again to continue. the steps are solid so one cannot see the drop below but of course you can look out as you go round. i managed this by focussing on the central post of the staircase and talking encouragingly to myself! if you are anxious about this you can probably bypass the cave paintings and head straight for the lions claw platform, although the paintings are interesting. another section leads up from the lions claws level to the top. this has iron sections crossing the rock, again with solid steps, but is more exposed. going up was easier as one faces the rock. i was more anxious about coming down but my husband went in front of me so i could hold on to his back with one hand and the railing with the other. the walkway gets quite crowded which slows the descent but means you are surrounded by people. this made me feel less exposed. i was nervous but it was very manageable. i have found other places more challenging like going up a tower in san giminiano and inside the dome of st pauls. i would make two other points- there are guides along the way who look out for people who look anxious and are quite insistent about holding your hand. kind but probably better declined. the remains at the top and the views are very impressive - well worth the effort - and if you get there with your fear of heights, a real achievement. i hope this is helpful - it would have helped me if i had been able to read this before i went.

if you are anxious about this you can probably bypass the cave paintings and head straight for the lions claw platform, although the paintings are interesting. another section leads up from the lions claws level to the top. this has iron sections crossing the rock, again with solid steps, but is more exposed. going up was easier as one faces the rock. i was more anxious about coming down but my husband went in front of me so i could hold on to his back with one hand and the railing with the other. the walkway gets quite crowded which slows the descent but means you are surrounded by people. this made me feel less exposed. i was nervous but it was very manageable. i have found other places more challenging like going up a tower in san giminiano and inside the dome of st pauls. i would make two other points- there are guides along the way who look out for people who look anxious and are quite insistent about holding your hand. kind but probably better declined. the remains at the top and the views are very impressive - well worth the effort - and if you get there with your fear of heights, a real achievement. i hope this is helpful - it would have helped me if i had been able to read this before i went.

review_text_clean: had a fun day at lion rock! this is a serious rock with a fascinating history but the climb is not for the faint-hearted or the unfit. as a 65yr old in decent condition it was still a reasonable challenge. there seemed to be some doing the climbing who may have under-estimated it. its 1-way up and 1-way down so turning back might be an issue. there are places to take a breather along the way. you should have good non-slip footwear, enough water, camera and as little to carry as possible. you will get hot and sweaty! having said all that....go for it! the view is spectacular! for others who dont feel up to the climb there is a museum and interesting parklands to walk thru. be warned of spruikers claiming to be official guides and who wont take no for an answer but i suppose can be helpful to assist the less agile.

review_text_clean: firstly, this point should be covered either early morning or later afternoon unless the weather is good. if it is hot, then you might not enjoy this place that much. coming to the place now. entry fee is 15 usd for saarc nations and 30 usd for others. i paid 2760 lkr per person. you have to walk for about 10 minutes to reach the point from where the climb begins. however, the place is extremely well managed and surpassed my expectations. it is a world heritage site and known as the eighth wonder. there are gardens and mini water bodies on both the sides. there is a very small bridge with water on both the sides just after the ticket checkpoint and one can have nice clicks standing on that. please do not throw away your tickets after this point since it is again checked midway into the ascent. coming to the climb, there are about 1200 steps. the difficulty is moderate. it surely tests your stamina. but if the weather is good, it is all worth it. as you keep on climbing, the view of entire surrounding just keeps on getting better. i doubt if you can get better views from any other place. it took us about 30-40 minutes to complete the climb. do not recollect noticing any restrooms on the way so be mindful of that. once you reach the top, you truly appreciate the work that has been done at such a height. it is a refreshing feeling at the top. you can easily spend an hour at the top, just sitting and roaming around. while climbing down, check with someone the way to tourist car parking area since that is different from the original place where your driver might have dropped you. it is must visit place. if the weather is on your side, then you will have an unforgettable time. this was the best sightseeing point for us on our entire sri lanka trip.
aspect_sentences: ['firstly, this point should be covered either early morning or later afternoon unless the weather is good.', 'but if the weather is good, it is all worth it.', 'if the weather is on your side, then you will have an unforgettable time.']

review_text_clean: sigiriya is one of the eight world heritage sites of sri lanka. it is one of the best preserved examples of ancient urban planning worldwide. there are remains of an extensive network of gardens and reservoirs. some structures like fountains are still intact today. the monolithic rock itself is a lava plug left over from an ancient long extinct volcano. it rises 200 m from the green scrub jungle surrounding it. today on top the visitor finds the ruins of what was once a kings fortress in the sky. while climbing up the steps there was a lady before us who got in the middle of a fight between a monkey and a dog. she got bitten by the dog and needed to go down to get treated by the red cross at the lions gate. this is nothing that you would like to happen to you. so be aware of stray dogs and over-curious monkeys. if they approach you too boldly you might want to try out a self defense technique marcell has discovered to be effective. he has successfully kept monkeys distant by using insect repellent.
aspect_sentences: ['she got bitten by the dog and needed to go down to get treated by the red cross at the lions gate.']
