review_text_clean: if you are in sri lanka and want to see lots of elephants and get up close and feed them, look no further than pinnawala elephant orphanage. about 2 to 2 12 hours drive from colombo is this nice, quiet area where they care for orphaned elephants. we could count more than two dozen elephants there. reach early i recommend leaving colombo by 6.30 if you want to capture it all when its not hot, and get tickets. as is with most places in sri lanka - entry ticket prices depend on your nationality. you walk in and the elephants come out and you can get close to the, feed them fruits etc. then they take the elephants for a shower at a nearby river. i thought it was going to be all natural, but then they opened a powerful hose and started showering the elephants. oh well.. sip a cup of coffee or get some juice while watching that at one of the few restaurants there watch out for those flies!. there are several shops that sell pooper paper made out of elephant poop and other trinkets there. i found them exorbitantly priced, so i skipped. but overall a very pleasant place to go outside of colombo.

review_text_clean: i visited pinnawala elephant orphanage on 15 february 2020 from australia. this was my first holiday to sri lanka even though my parents are sri lankan. i had heard many stories from my relatives about the elephants at pinnawala and had always wanted to visit. in saying that, making the decision to go was a tough one as i am aware that currently pinnawala is classed as slightly controversial i am an extreme animal lover! nevertheless after reading many reviews some from people whom havent even visited the site!?, i decided that i needed to see it for myself make up my own mind. my honest opinion was that i was pleasantly surprised and i believe that they are genuinely trying to improve the operations of the park. out of the 90 odd elephants i saw there, the majority were free roaming and appeared to enjoy their free time and bathing in the river. the only elephants i saw had chains were some of the males which is more for everyones protection so as not to cause a stampede. there were also 2 that were in pens apparently under veterinary care. the only tourist interaction that i saw was the fruit feeding which i avidly took part in - i bought like 4 baskets of fruit to give to 2 beautiful elephants. and for those people complaining about having to pay for the fruit baskets- get over it! it only costs like 2 aud for a basket of fruit! you pay way more than that for animal encounters in western countries and thats not included in your ticket price either! no tourists that i saw were allowed to bathe with the elephants etc at the park and i didnt really see any exploitation as such. ie, i did not see any elephant rides being provided. it was just a joy to see them down at the river with many elephants enjoying the water or their mud bath. at the end of the day people will need to make up their own minds as to what theyre comfortable with. i personally am happy i went there and i dont believe it is as bad as some people are making it out to be.
aspect_sentences: ['you pay way more than that for animal encounters in western countries and thats not included in your ticket price either!']

review_text_clean: today we travelled a long way especially to visit the pinnawala elephant orphanage and we were so disappointed. it was 3,000lhr to enter and we specifically went for 1pm as between 12pm-2pm that you can supposedly feed the elephants fruit and see milking time. we walked in and the place was deserted, there was no one to help direct you or advise you, only some signs. there were a few elephants you could see in a small grass area with a couple of trees which you could see from a viewing point at least 15 metres away from the elephants themselves. we moved along to another area where there were 6 males chained up to a tiny concrete area with nothing but a couple of coconuts on the floor and men clearing up the ground around them. they were clearly very distressed and not happy in their environment and it was extremely sad to see this especially as we had believed this was somewhere they look after the animals well. there was no elephants in the fruit feeding enclosure we also saw this was an extra charge even if there was all in all we were there for about 15 minutes before we decided we should leave. if you love animals and want to see elephants being treated well in a safe environment do not bother wasting your time.
aspect_sentences: ['if you love animals and want to see elephants being treated well in a safe environment do not bother wasting your time.']

review_text_clean: i was more than shocked. on the one hand we only wanted to watch the animals bathing and we were told that we need a ticket for 3000 lkr each there is a ticket office for tourists and locals. i doubt that they are the same prices which is not correct. you can just walk down to the river between 10am and 12pm or 2pm and 4 pm and watch the elephants bathing. you need the ticket to see the orphanage, which was one of the saddest things i have ever seen. the animals have far too little space and no things to play with. when we asked why two elephants were chained and kept circling their heads, we were told their will first has to be broken. there was also an enclosure with 3 baby elephants inside, which were made to pose for photos. there were men standing in front of it offering to take photos of us and the elephants. however, this is not a nice gesture even if the locals are otherwise very nice and helpful, but afterwards the hand is held out again for money. also the small elephants which are rescued are not let back into freedom. once an elephant is in pinnawala, it never leaves again. some of the elephants were chained to the river and many men with very sharp sticks were also on guard. of course safety is a must. but i didnt have a good feeling. better to go to the udawalawe national park and see elephants without chains and men with pointed lances. later we also talked to a very good english speaking local, who told us that only a small part of the income goes to the animals
aspect_sentences: ['i doubt that they are the same prices which is not correct.']

review_text_clean: im not too sure what i thought about this place. the elephants have been rescued and they appear happy enough but i had the vague feeling thye were like peforming elephants in a zoo. it is a geat expeirence to being down a thoroughfre and suddenly a small herd of elephants with their handlers wlk past you. it was great too to see them behaving quite natrally in the water. but there were some moments of disquiet. some of the elephants are chained, and i accept and understand why, but it does leave an impression. a couple of the elephants are also forced to lie down in the water for the benefit of the crowd which i was not sure of either. still, it was an experience althougha bit expensive, 3000 rupees per foreigner. if you want the experience of feeding a quiet elephant, you can also do that for 250 rupees. there are no elephant rides and i was pleased about that. finally watch out for a scam with the mahouts handlers. they will try to isolate you away from the crowd and lead you up into an area by yourself. they then offer to photograph you with an elephant by yourself but wont return your cameraiphone until you pay them money. i was offered this a couple of times but did not do it. i did see a family forking out a few thousand rupees to one of them so watch out for it.
aspect_sentences: ['it is a geat expeirence to being down a thoroughfre and suddenly a small herd of elephants with their handlers wlk past you.', 'it was great too to see them behaving quite natrally in the water.']

review_text_clean: this place was not originally on our iternary but our driver suggested it and it was on our way almost to dambulla. im glad we stopped here. it is sad to see them in chains but this is a treatment centre for injured elephants. we got to feed meenachi, the elephant. i should confess this is the first time i actually touched an elephant. after the feeding, the elephants were taken to a river across to bathe. how is elephants bathing in a river not a viral video on youtube is beyond me. its was an absolute delight to watch these elephants frolic in the river. we couldnt sit and watch for hours to keep up with our iternary. on our way out we stopped buy to pick-up poo-poo paper. yes its paper made out of elephant dung. dont worry it doesnt smell. i suggest to bargain before buying or wait till kandy to purchase. we found poo-poo paper cheaper in galle dutch fort and kandy.

review_text_clean: we went here wanting to make up our own minds from reading reviews and have very mixed feelings. on one hand, the elephants were healthy looking no bones showing and majority allowed to roam around the river free. however, around 8 elephants were chained to various spots around the river...the signs say this is to stop harmdanger of the male elephants. from the looks of things, these elephants were chained for tourists photos as they were dotted around the hotel points and only need the front of the viewing platform. the elephants are also clearly scared of the mahouts when one of them began to ride the elephant he was nearly kicked off. we went up to the relaxing zone which didnt look that way for the elephants at all. it sort of looks like an elephant zoo enclosure, however yet again all elephants there were chained up and visibly distressed. a better idea would be to let the elephants freely roam and invite tourists to visit safari style - no touching or contact. what we couldnt understand is if this was an orphanage...why arent they let out into the wild, given they are well enoughold enough.
aspect_sentences: ['the elephants are also clearly scared of the mahouts when one of them began to ride the elephant he was nearly kicked off.']

review_text_clean: pinnawala elephant orphanage is an orphanage located at pinnawala village approximately 13km from kegalle town on the colombo kandy road a1 turn to left near the 82km post. this orphanage provides a lifeline to the orphaned baby elephants and orphaned elephants lost in the wilderness. you can see them having a bath in the river then crossed the road back to the orphanage where they are feed and roam the ground. the orphanage will be open from 08.30 hrs to 18.00 hrs daily. normally herd of elephants bathing in the river from 10.00 to 12.00 again from 14.00 to 16.00. milk feeding starts in morning 09.15, 13.15 and 17.00 hrs. it is the place that gives us unforgettable experience. elephant caretakers must care with love and respect without being cruel to the elephants will help them grow up with nature.

review_text_clean: so disappointed with pinnawala elephant orphanage. they advertise saying elephants are semi wild but reality is, elephants are not well treated, elephants have mahouts to be trained and unfortunately they dont have a proper semiwild life. elephants will end working for temples and going to parahera in some point which makes me really sad. pinnawala orphanage says there are 84 elephants but visible you can only see a group of 27 elephants other group of 10 sick elephants. where are the others? i would say, chained, because they refuse to be domesticated i paid 3k rupees for the entrance expecting to see elephants having a better care. i am the person who would pay more if elephants are well treated. elephants only eat once per day kindly note elephants of pinnawala are well fitted, but still, the nature of elephants is to eat several times per day. sri lanka government, please do something to improve the programs for elephants, i understand your mindset, culture and religion and most important i respect it, i understand the value and meaning of parahera, but dont advertise lies. please give a better care for them. elephants are humble and loyal animals we should be better for them. note some elephants are on their musth period, is understandable that they remain separated from the group, but, are 50 elephants on their musth? dont think so. note 2 tourism is an income that pinnawala orphanage needs to give elephants a better life. i wont say dont visit the place, i will say go and see for yourself, raise the voice and ask sri lanka government to improve the programs.

review_text_clean: we arrived in the late morning and found most of the elephants down at the river bathing. as we walked down the street to see them, we passed several shops selling souvenirs and then suddenly were treated to a few elephants being ridden back to the orphanage from the river. it was a bit scary, but also exciting as they walked right past us. we got down to the river and there was the rest of the group bathing and playing. we took a few pictures and then went to the orphanage where after a short walk inside we came to an area where one can feed the elephants. i didnt see any mistreatment while we were there, but our experience was limited to about an hour and a half. its a long drive to get here, but if you like elephants, its worth the drive. we also passed a few wild elephants crossing the road on the way from colombo, so keep an eye out if this is your route too.

review_text_clean: if you short of time andor money, you can easily avoid this place. this is basically a zoo even worse than a zoo than an orphanage. how often do you see children in orphanage tied up with chains and made to walk a long alleyway just so that a few tourists who paid exorbitant prices for tickets can watch them walk and feed them coconuts? the elephants take bath in the pond which is at the opposite side of the road from the orphanage, twice a day. we were very excited that we reached just in time when the elephants were getting ready to walk through that alley to go to the pond to take bath. what we saw was very disappointing. almost all the elephants were chained to their teeth. most of them were missing their tusks dont know when it happened and almost all of them just sat in the pond and did nothing. inside the orphanage, it was the same story. you can see them grazing or can give them bananas or other fruits there are extra charges for that as you can only buy the fruits from one of the shops inside the orphanage. we were from the saarc country so we paid 750 lkr per person for entry but i think for foreign tourists from other countries the fees is around 3000 lkr. it is highly overpriced and its better to actually go to marissa and watch whales in their natural habitat instead of seeing chained elephants sitting in water. you can do all the things you can do here at dehiwala zoo in colombo, including seeing elephants taking bath.

review_text_clean: we visited this place in february as part of a tour with mercury holidays. we were hoping it would be the highlight of our trip, sadly it left us with bad memories for this part of the trip. we started watching the elephants in the water from an adjacent hotel veranda, the elephants certainly didnt appear to want to be there, they were corralled to stay close to the hotels so that visitors could see them. we then went to the land site on the opposite side of the road, again elephants are corralled for the entertainment of the viewing public. a very heavily pregnant elephant was trying to get to a water hole at the top of the paddock with some other elephants following, however the mahouts would not let her rest and drove her and her followers to the part of the paddock closest to the tourists. in another part of the paddock one of the mahouts was repeatedly hitting an elephant in the leg making it squeal, a sound i dont want to hear again. one of the staff stood near me kept saying happy elephant. im not david attenborough but i would say that the elephant was not squealing with delight. there were also other elephants under shelter which clearly had mental issues and were heavily chained, i do however appreciate that where they have been rescued from may be the cause of their problems and not the place they have come to. i have read through some of the reviews and they do vary widely and of course theyre all personal assessments, some cultures approach animal care differently, for instance some have referred to being able to ride the elephants which i personally dont agree with. i would strongly recommend you think seriously about visiting this place, yes there are a lot of elephants here which is great, but the evident lack of care for them is distressing if you are an animal lover.

review_text_clean: despite all the positive recommendations for this elephant orphanage, it seemed more like an elephant medium security prison. there are many captive elephants that are kept in large fields. in some areas the visitors can come close and even touch the tamer elephants. around mid morning 1030 to be precise, the elephants are paraded down to the nearby river and encouraged or in the case of some of the young male bulls, forced to bathe. the male elephants are chained up and pushed and prodded, and appear and sound unhappy. the females and children though are allowed to roam and appear less anxious. in comparison to elephant sanctuaries in thailand or free roaming african elephants, many of these asian elephants appeared to be distinctly unhappy and uncomfortable. we went with two teenage girls and they were distinctly unhappy with the elephants circumstances, as was i.

review_text_clean: we visited this elephant orphanage and quite honestly didnt see any ill treatment of the animals. it was lovely to see the elephants walking to the river for a bathe. we got quite close to a few of the cheeky ones who came up to the chain where we could stand. yes a few of the males have a chain to a leg but we were told they were the frisky ones and it was to help keep them under control. the older males are separated from the females as in the wild . they even have a murderer male which is kept apart from all the others and needs a few members of staff around when cleaning his area. he apparently has killed humans when he was in the wildlife reserves- so nice to see he has been given a chance to life as his rages were probably instigated by humans who didnt behave appropriately around him. we were told not to buy fruit from the street sellers and were always reminded to behave appropriately. such a joy to see these huge creatures.
aspect_sentences: ['we visited this elephant orphanage and quite honestly didnt see any ill treatment of the animals.', 'such a joy to see these huge creatures.']

review_text_clean: some negative reviews on here and comments concerning the treatment of the elephants. some are in chains but these are male elephants and are to control their natural aggression to other males. the mahmoods use sticks to encourage understanding of commands - again for the safety of the elephants and surrounding people. they use the sticks to apply pressure to vital points acupuncture points which do not harm the elephants - if youve ever been struck in a pressure point you will know a slight jab doesnt hurt but does encourage the body to move in a certain way. this is what they do with the sticks. you couldnt move an elephant with a shove or a little stick otherwise. if youre concerned with the treatment suggest research first before judging. many of the elephants come from farmland where theyve been trapped in holes dug by farmers to collect water. they often have broken limbs when they come to the sanctuary. once recovered, most are returned to the forests. some pictures attached of the time we watched them bathing. one thing to note - from wherever you are you will likely take some time to get there. for us it was worth the journey.
aspect_sentences: ['some negative reviews on here and comments concerning the treatment of the elephants.', 'if youre concerned with the treatment suggest research first before judging.']

review_text_clean: i strongly recommend skipping this experience. there are so many great opportunities to see elephants in their natural habitat in sri lanka. this was not an orphanage, more like a zoo. the staff did not appear to care about the animals. the animals are not treated well. they dont seem to have the freedom to roam that i hoped they would. they are chained up at times. standing in the river, they were made to stand in a tight group. the website advertises bottle feeding but this is no longer happening. we were approached by an employee who offered to take a photo. he then led us behind a building we thought he was leading us to more elephants and demanded a tip. our kids did enjoy feeding fruit to the elephants. still, not the experience we were hoping for.
aspect_sentences: ['there are so many great opportunities to see elephants in their natural habitat in sri lanka.', 'the animals are not treated well.']

review_text_clean: we visited this tour part of what mercury holidays offer, i did at the time question the rep about the chains on the elephannts as i had read about this, and aware this is a cultural difference, but at the end of the day it should be about the elephant not a zoo or making the elephant perform for you. the rep advised the chains were required as the bulls do get aggressive. what i dont understand is elephants should be able to roam freely, however when we visited i was sad to see these poor animals in such distress. when you approach the orphanage you are advised not to purchase any fruit but to buy inside, the place was heaving with local school children coach loads - not sure if this is part of their school curriculum but vast amount visiting. the elephants in the watering hole seemed dazed and when one elephant approach the handler who has a stick with a hook to control the elephants came close she quickly reacted and walked away - the elephants seemed lifeless and bored. one elephant was showing signs of distress side to side shaking her head and body - not nice to see. we then visited the feeding stations and walked passed where the elephants are seen my the public - makes you wonder how much space do these elephants have to roam - not a great deal. i saw the bull elephants chained and what was so shocking was the behaviour again rocking back and forth - this is where he remains all day - and the phrase for the wealth and safety of all elephants was the reason - this was utterly sad, such a beautiful animal chained. again aware the cultural differences but, somehow human instinct should kick in for anyone to see these elephants are anything but happy. we then visited the feeding station once again for the elephants to perform - one of the man handlers asked if i wanted a picture of the elephant raising its trunk - he called the elephant over and used this stick to control her - just like a circus act, and she had chains around her neck. please think twice about contributing to this orphanage in hindsight i regret contributing, and my advice would be be go on the safari - this is where you see elephants roaming freely and happy but the choice is yours.
aspect_sentences: ['we then visited the feeding stations and walked passed where the elephants are seen my the public - makes you wonder how much space do these elephants have to roam - not a great deal.']

review_text_clean: i visited pinnawala elephant orphanage just over a week ago and i must say that i was on high alert after a few derogatory articles i had seen written about the facility and its treatment of the elephants. happily, i found nothing worthy of a complaint. the elephants parade down to the river and anyone who knows animals can see that they are intelligent beings who are used to the routine and are not at all stressed by the watching crowds - in fact, some clearly loved it and were happy to participate and be patted or fed a morsel along the way. once in the river they splash, roll around in the water and clearly enjoy themselves. yes, some did have a loose chain around their necks, but this didnt bother them. when you consider the size of an elephant and the general havoc they could cause to a community when aggressive, its not difficult to understand that there are times when they must be prudently restrained or separated. as for returning them all to the wild these elephants no longer have a place in the wild as they have formed new family bonds within their new herd. many have already been rescued from the wild where they were close to death and others are on medication or special food. so if you want to truly help elephants and not just have a pompous rant about turning them loose, visit pinnawala, spend a few dollars towards their support and watch them happily splash about in safety.

review_text_clean: reviews of pinnawala elephant orphanage praise and condemn so our only choice was to see it for ourselves. the stamp of the countrys department of wildlife conservation on the park was the deciding factor. over a twenty year period, pinnawala elephant orphanage hand raised abandoned babies, treated the injured and integrated displaced elephants into a growing herd. currently, 88 elephants are part of the pinnawala family on their 30-acre property, making it one of sri lankas largest tourist attractions. at pinnawala elephant orphanage you will see chains. this is precautionary for large males while bathing, wandering the park river path, and when a females seductive pheromones spike. a full grown male can stand more than 2.5 metres weighing 5.5 tonnes. a force to be reckoned with when they want to get down to business. you will also see mahouts rounding the elephants to keep them in one spot. this is also precautionary to keep them from getting too close to punters. a disappointing observation was people paying some entrepreneurial mahouts to bathe the elephants. the elephant is chained and made to lie on its side during the encounter. this is not approved and is something the orphanage is trying to eliminate. elephants eat an average of 250kg of food per day, multiply that by 88 of them and you have an expensive grocery bill. modern veterinary equipment and traditional indigenous medicine come at a price and the gallons of milk required to raise a baby elephant is also exorbitant. sponsorship programs, donations and your ticket price all contribute to the cost of feeding and caring for these adorable creatures. pinnawala elephant orphanage is not perfect, but the care for these elephants is obvious. this is a heavily tourist-trafficked attraction. vendors take advantage of the captive audience and sell everything from elephant poo paper products quite an interesting process to every form of elephant printed clothing you can imagine. away from this retail madness, however, is picturesque countryside, a meandering river and comfortable accommodation.

review_text_clean: having read some of the reviews on here i approached this visit with caution. but i was pleasantly surprised. sure, it no longer operates as an orphanage but a controlled breeding zoo. that said, the elephants seemed well cared for and minimally managed by the mahouts. i never saw any being mistreated. yes some are temporarily chained for the safety of the herd and human safety. so long as they control the matriarch andor bull the rest will generally follow. its easy to judge but the govt agency has a big elephant population to manage throughout the country with very little funding, all in various states, wild working, and in different relationships with humans.
aspect_sentences: ['i never saw any being mistreated.']

review_text_clean: spent 2 weeks volunteering here as a family so gained some insight into the orphanage. the orphanage would love to see all elephants in the wild, unfortunately this is impossible with pressures on land use by a growing population. they cant introduce elephants to an existing wild herd as they would not be accepted. all elephants in the orphanage have been raised in captivity so would seek out people if released and this would in turn create conflict risking the elephants life. the mahouts do shout and use ashoks with elephants to ensure public safety. to see behind the public face and watch them tenderly go over the elephants skin for 2 hours looking for problems shows their true feelings towards the animals. they shout at the cleaners if the elephant houses are not sufficiently cleaned. the prices are fair for tourists and cheaper for locals to encourage locals to visit, learn and take an interest in their own wildlife. this is a government run organisation so the prices are set in colombo, not by the orphanage. the extra fee for feeding or bathing elephants is likewise set by the politicians. the elephant in the room - chains. these are necessary to manage the herd in a small area to keep public, staff and elephants safe. injured, sick and pregnant elephants are kept separate, but still taken for free time at the river away from the main herd. there are 19 elephants housed here which have been seized from illegal owners and are awaiting court cases so cant be put with the herd. in all we really enjoyed our 2 weeks here giving us an insight not gained during a short visit. volunteering is hard work and not for everybody. we learnt about the politics behind a lot of decisions and saw the love held for these wonderful creatures by all the staff at the orphanage.

review_text_clean: i wish i had done my research before going to the pinnawala elephant orphanage because it was honestly more like a prison than an orphanage. the second we got there we were bombarded by a man who said after we see the elephants eat we need to get in a tuk tuk to see the elephants bathe and then go to the spice factory. you do not have to do this! all you need to do is cross the street to see the elephants bathe. now back to this horrible place.... once we entered everything just seemed like an amusement park. it seems this place is more for making money than helping animals. most of the animals were chained up not able to roam free. there was also an area for i guess the elephants that could not be with the rest of the population and they were chained in an area that was dark and smellyand they were weaving back and forth. this is a sign of distress which many of the elephants exhibited. once it was time for the elephants to bathe in the water they walked them down in chains while the handlers prodded them with their bull hooks. i was shocked to see how aggressive they were with the elephants. if the wanted the elephant to move or stand a certain way they would hit it with a wooden stick then take the hook part and stab the head of the elephants. you could see when the handlers came around the elephants were scared. i also saw them prodding elephants to pick things up and move them. they were using them for work abs using the hooks to get them to do what they wanted. it was an extremely sad and disturbing place. if you love animals do not give your money and support this torturous place. this is just a place to exploit elephants and make money. i have to give 1 star to post this but it would have been 0 stars.

review_text_clean: i had read up about pinnawala elephant orphanage before i visited sri lanka and from what id read, i was honestly considering skipping the visit due to claims of animal abuse and unnecessary confinement. but as it turned out, i was part of a group and because the group wanted to go, i had little option but to tag along. what i saw there truly horrified me. 1. elephant calves were confined in a circular pen and their legs tied with metal chains that left little room for manoeuvre or free movement. 2. there was a tusker displaying a classic case of depressive symptoms - head swaying incessantly and bobbing up and down. like the calves, he was also tied with a short metal chain in a small shed. 3. a herd of elephants we saw there was so scared of the keeper that as soon as he entered the enclosure with his bull-hook, the terrified elephants literally fled away from him. the keeper was careful not to display any aggressive behaviour in front of the tourists but it was obvious from how scared the elephants were, that terrible things go on behind the scenes. 4. while there, we saw a keeper repeatedly strike a pregnant elephant with a huge pole that had a metal spike at its end. he poked and struck her hard despite the presence of tourists there. i cannot imagine what must be going on once tourist hours are over. we then headed off to the river adjacent to the orphanage where they take the elephants for a bath - hoping that at least there, the elephants must be free. but they were not. even here, the elephants were tied with short chains while tourists threw fruit at them. i wouldve compared pinnawala elephant orphanage to a zoo but most zoos treat their animals better than this orphanage does. pinnawala is not a place i would ever visit again. my money isnt going into a place that has made a business out of abusing animals that shouldve been returned to the wild. plus, they breed elephants in confinement at pinnawala. real orphanages dont typically do that. instead, i would strongly recommend visiting the elephant transit home near udawalawe national park. i havent been there but from what ive heard, they are much more responsible in caring for orphaned elephants. plus they return the elephants to the wild once they are old enough - unlike pinnawala.

head swaying incessantly and bobbing up and down. like the calves, he was also tied with a short metal chain in a small shed. 3. a herd of elephants we saw there was so scared of the keeper that as soon as he entered the enclosure with his bull-hook, the terrified elephants literally fled away from him. the keeper was careful not to display any aggressive behaviour in front of the tourists but it was obvious from how scared the elephants were, that terrible things go on behind the scenes. 4. while there, we saw a keeper repeatedly strike a pregnant elephant with a huge pole that had a metal spike at its end. he poked and struck her hard despite the presence of tourists there. i cannot imagine what must be going on once tourist hours are over. we then headed off to the river adjacent to the orphanage where they take the elephants for a bath - hoping that at least there, the elephants must be free. but they were not. even here, the elephants were tied with short chains while tourists threw fruit at them. i wouldve compared pinnawala elephant orphanage to a zoo but most zoos treat their animals better than this orphanage does. pinnawala is not a place i would ever visit again. my money isnt going into a place that has made a business out of abusing animals that shouldve been returned to the wild. plus, they breed elephants in confinement at pinnawala. real orphanages dont typically do that. instead, i would strongly recommend visiting the elephant transit home near udawalawe national park. i havent been there but from what ive heard, they are much more responsible in caring for orphaned elephants. plus they return the elephants to the wild once they are old enough - unlike pinnawala.

review_text_clean: the orphanage has three broad time slots milk feeding to calves, fruit feeding to elephants, elephant bathing, so you should try to plan your arrival at beginning of one of these picture has details, zoom in. you will be shuffling between hold area for feeding and river for bathing. one ticket rs. 700 saarc country, rs. 2500 for other countries, 50 for children gets you multiple access to all events. you can easily spend 2-3 hours here watching elephants eat, play, relax, dance, and what not. they even have huge hose spraying elephants in the river, though we expected more frolicking in water it was still good experience. there are various souvenir shops and elephant poo paper shops around, and few mid-range restaurants. story behind orphanage is that it takes care of abandoned calves and tends them to youth, though for tourist purposes you can consider it open zoo. there is also separate zoo nearby and you can also take elephant ride. lot of negative reviews are from people who are aghast seeing animals in chains. its not a jungle safari, and some elephants are in chains some of the time. go for watching elephants doing various things, as extended version of zoo. dont go thinking its natural habitat. its always ironically funny to see bleeding heart of meat eaters for animal cruelity.

review_text_clean: both my partner and i are animal lovers, and we deliberated long and hard whether to visit here due to some of the trip advisor reviews. however, after doing more research and reading some independant travel articles, we decided to visit - and i am glad we did. yes, there are chains used to anchor, help control and keep the elephants safe as well as the many visitors this place has. in addition, the males - especially when in musth - need to be controlled and seperated. these elephants can never be released in to the wild, so ensuring they can not wander off when in the river is essential. i did not see any evidence of distress, and i saw some lovely interactions in the main herd with some of the younger ones playing. they genuinely seemed to enjoy their time in the river, and seeing them walk through the main street was an experience! this place is not perfect - however people also need to remember this is a poor country. it seems to me like they try and do the best they can with the money that is available. the only thing that stood out to me is that the mahouts seemed to over use their hooks and shout when it did not seem necessary. this could be my ignorance of course, but it seemed over the top at times like they were showing off to the crowds.
aspect_sentences: ['it seems to me like they try and do the best they can with the money that is available.']

review_text_clean: i dont even handle an orphan baby like this. elephants are most brainy animals in this world and when you see elephant babies with their herd, you can figure out how they are protected by other elephants. the initiative is very good by the government, but commercialising this is not a fair approach to that baby elephants. animal lovers especially those study about elephants and its emotions will understand this. the elephants are not treated as babies or orphans. they are mainly managed to attract the tourist who visit that place. locals who belongs to this place, including the management and staff should at least show the attitude of their loving approach to elephants. as a human if you have never seen elephants closely or interacted with baby elephants, you may find this place interesting. we have lived in a culture southern most part of india which is very much similar to lanka, with elephants on day to day life. in timber depot, temple festivals, local rich guys house, but baby one is always attraction for us. we arrived around 1030 by the time the babies were at the river playing, some were afraid of the crowd being gathered, some are weak to even taking bath play. we also saw while they were taking back to the so called orphanage from river. pros- you can see herds of babies in one go. cons- you wont see the feel of orphan baby elephant being well treated. more of a commercial establishment to sell substances, gift items with elephant name or photo somewhere. but a place one should visit at least once, best time is while they were going to river, taking bath and coming back. timings are displayed and published in their web page. avoid buying souvenirs from their, as the prices are sky-rocketed for tourists. you will find same items in cheaper rates outside.

review_text_clean: ive got very mixed feelings about pinnawala. on the one hand - beautiful to see so many elephants together in safety. some reviewers have stated that all the elephants are in chains - they are not. the information boards clearly explain that the male elephants are chained when in the public areas for the safety of everyone around them. however, i did see an area with two baby elephants who were chained front and back, unsupervised, surrounded by noisy tourists. i didnt stay long to see this, it was too upsetting. things that bothered me were - what happens to the adult male elephants? where do they go? are the elephants ever released back into the wild? regardless, this is a beautiful place, surrounded by hills, with the most elephants youre ever likely to see in one place.
aspect_sentences: ['ive got very mixed feelings about pinnawala.']

review_text_clean: there are clearly divided opinions about places such as these. the elephants here are either orphan elephants, those born in captivity or ex-working elephants in retirement. they are cared for at the orphanage their whole lives and are not planned for release back into the wild, as they probably would not survive by themselves, having become accustomed to human handling. we saw them taken to the river for their daily bathing, and clearly they enjoyed the experience, playing and splashing around with each other and even trying to mate! in the water for several hours.. some in our group objected to the chains the elephants wear and the actions of the mahouts prodding them to move. we learned later contrary to appearances the elephants are not chained up back in the orphanage - they only have the chains on for use in an emergency and for public protection if they get spooked. but as one commentator has already said, if you want to see elephants in a free and natural environment, visit one of the many national parks - not the orphanage, or a sanctuary.

review_text_clean: before our trip to sri lanka i did a lot of research online into pinnawala elephant orphanage. there are lots of contrasting opinions online so in the end we decided to visit. i regret going here and giving this company my money. the elephants are not well looked after, they are paraded around like zoo animals, and patrolled with bull hooks and chains and it is a massive money making exercise. the elephants here are not happy, and there is no program to release the orphans back into the wild. i came away feeling really sad and sorry for the elephants at this place. if you are thinking about visiting - please do not! instead save your money and go on a safari at minneriya national park, where you will see hundreds of happy elephants in their natural habitat.
aspect_sentences: ['instead save your money and go on a safari at minneriya national park, where you will see hundreds of happy elephants in their natural habitat.']

review_text_clean: we got there at bath time. elephants seemed to enjoy being in the river. they were given reasonable room to roam, a 30m x 10m section of river. a few wandered past the handlers to forage on the far side of the river ... it seemed that they could have made a dash for freedom into the forests, but they didnt. of herd of 30, only 2 or 3 had chains. handlers had hooked poles but although they were waved around, i did not see any physical abuse or contact. we enjoyed seeing them close up and being relatively free in the river. these are not wild elephants. not sure what happens at other times or the conditions in which they are kept. would be sad if they were not treated well then. although we sat on the hotel balcony, there was no pressure on us to buy drinks etc.
aspect_sentences: ['would be sad if they were not treated well then.']

review_text_clean: there are a lot of misleading reviews about pinnawala. ive been twice - earlier this month and 21 years ago - and ive enjoyed the experience both times. the price of 2500 rupees about 11 per person is quite high but much lower than ive seen online where its often stated at 20 per person. theres not too much to do. our driver went in with us which we thought a bit odd until we realised he knew exactly where to go and when to make sure we got the best experience. we went first to the elephant paddocks where the ladies were hanging around eating and waiting for bath time. in a separate area, the boys were getting ready to go the river. nothing can really prepare you for seeing a massive herd of elephants on the move. the boys went first, strolling through the orphanage, out to the road and down to the river. some are chained - for their safety and everybody elses. i dont think its a bad thing. once the boys were on their way, the lady elephants followed. we watched the bath time for nearly 2 hours. our driver urged us to a brilliant watching space in a cafe which we really appreciated. in two hours you have plenty of time to watch and observe the different personalities amongst the elephants. there are the cheeky younger boys, the stubborn old ladies, the frisky and the laid-back all hanging out together. people have commented on the use of spikes or guides. we was the metal guides being used by the mahoots but always very gently and never with any violence. the love of the handlers for their pachyderm pals was clear to all. one old lady - quite possibly the grande dame of the herd - spent an hour standing knee deep trying to avoid a wash. her mahoot gently urged her into deeper water, taking his time and using his guide to help scrape old mud off her head and back. eventually she gave in and rolled over in the water to let him clean her properly. some are chained in the water but didnt seem distressed about it. a couple of young females made a jovial bid for freedom on the far banks and were laughingly chased down and returned to the herd. if youre looking for lots of action, this may disappoint. if you have the patience to watch and wait, youll probably love it as much as i did. one comment. i think the management should consider rebranding this as an elephant home rather than an elephant orphanage since it seems to create elevated expectations of lots of babies and at present there really arent many at all. the purpose of the home is to give safe haven to elephants, not to go looking for unwanted babies. back in the days of the civil war, a lot of babies were orphaned by their parents being killed accidentally or intentionally so there were more little ones to see. these days they do have a few babies but i suspect thats more an outcome of boy and girl elephants getting friendly rather than any kind of captive breeding programme.

review_text_clean: we visited pinnawala elephant orphanage again, the first time was 2007, certainly another highlight was according to our guide there are nearly 100 orphaned elephants here and we got to see them be playful with each other, walk through the sanctuary, saw them being fed milk members of the public can do this but there is only a limited number of tickets available, if i recall rightly its only 30, what an unbelievable sight it is to see them walking down the street towards the river for their bathing 10-12 and 2-4. they blow a siren warns of approaching elephants to signal that the elephants are on the way, you can stand within 2 feet or so of the procession. once safe, make your way back to the rocks by the water. this is an excellent vantage point to enjoy the spectacle. when all merchants guided all tourists inside and took their merchandise inside as well. then dozens of elephants marched through the 200m market street and some bags and t-shirts feel down to the ground as they had passed by so close to the shops including the poo shop. the keepers or mahouts also carry guide sticks to help direct the elephants to the bathing river etc. they never hit or hurt the elephants with these sticks, they just use them gently to guide them safely across the roads etc. then we positioned ourselves on the verandah of the hotel, where to also had lunch overlooking the river got a really good view of the elephants being washed playing in the water.
aspect_sentences: ['then we positioned ourselves on the verandah of the hotel, where to also had lunch overlooking the river got a really good view of the elephants being washed playing in the water.']

review_text_clean: it was very sad to see some of the elephants chained in solitary confinement. the reason that they are adults and may pose a threat to others at certain times does not seem a true statement. this as supposed to be an orphanage but it is clearly also a breeding program. we were told that the animals are never released into the wild, surely other species can be rehabilitated so that seemed so wrong. we went to see the animals bathing in the river and were disgusted to see a young elephant walked down the road heavily chained and tethered to a rock when in the water, it was clearly distressed and only settled when an older one was allowed near it. many of the others were chained to rings embedded on the rocks. most of them didnt seem too stressed by this but i suppose they dont know any other life.
aspect_sentences: ['the reason that they are adults and may pose a threat to others at certain times does not seem a true statement.']

review_text_clean: i was so looking forward to seeing the elephants. at first it looks lovely when you get to the elephants, they are all in the river, but i started looking closely and noticed one elephant on his own at the back on his own, he looked very distressed swaying from side to side and chained down. i tried to ask questions but no one wanted to answer me! then there was another one with the herd that was also chained down. the mahuttes have sticks with sharp ends on them, the elephants did not look relaxed i come away feeling very angry and upset. when you visit the orphanage across the road, there were 4 males chained down in the park, this should not happen, again when you ask questions you get excuses, like they need to do this for safety reasons. i never got to see them feed or wash them that was at a different time, so i cannot comment. not sure you should visit this park, there are lots of other parks where the elephants are wild, i i feel its for tourists, not sure i would call it an orphanage??

review_text_clean: read a lot of extreme comments of this site beforehand. this place was highly recommended by the agent and was a midpoint from capital to dambulla. we spent an hour here for a short walk with the elephant, feed with fruit, and watched it at bath in the river. each elephant had an assigned caretaker to look after and as per the guide, the elephant would only be chained at night during sleep and no wounds or marks could be found at the elephant leg which caused by the chain. literally there was no evident to prove if they treated the elephant in a proper manner or not in just an hour stay. to us, this spot could be omitted as we would visit minneriya national park seeing the wild elephant 2 days after this. recommend to go for the wild elephant instead of seeing the caged.

review_text_clean: we stayed in negombo and it was a 2 hour drive from our hotel to the elephant orphanage, along the way we visited the herbal garden and a tea factory. it was nice to see the elephants bathing in the river, the baby elephants feeding wasnt really worth it. you just see the caretaker fill a bottle with milk and then the elephant drinks it in less than 10 seconds! you cannot really pet the elephants, but they do have a feeding area, however by the time we got there the food finished. you dont get a one on one experience with the elephants as there are lots of tourists around. there are several shops around to buy souvenirs. i especially liked the shop that sold elephant poo paper they show you a quick demonstration of how its made. very interesting and worth a quick visit and purchase! i recommend visiting the elephant orphanage.

review_text_clean: first things first, i saw no evidence of any physical abuse of the elephants during my visit to pinnewala orphanage. the elephants look well fed, clean and have no scars from chains or sticks as far as i could see. the keepers used goads to guide the elephants and to prevent the bulls trying to mix with the main herd of femalesyounger elephants, but i did not see a single one being hit. the chains used on some of the bulls look unpleasant, but they seem to be loosely fitted and not particularly irritating to the animals. keeping such large and potentially aggressive animals under control is essential when they are in such close proximity to one another bulls generally wouldnt mix with the herd in the wild and to humans. the animals are corralled to be fed and kept in a certain quite large area of the river to be washed, but otherwise roam around a large natural reserve. some of the extras put on for tourists photos with the elephants, feedingwashing them etc arent acceptable. the elephants are wild animals, not playthings or props, and they should be treated as such. a couple of keepers rode some of the bulls back from the river, which again i dont agree with. additionally, perhaps more effort could be made to return some of the animals back to the wild, however i dont know anything about the practicalities and of course this runs the risk of them being killed by farmers the main threat to wild elephants in sri lanka. all in all, as far as i could tell the pinnewala orphanage is not abusive to the animals in its care and is no worse than western zoos. keeping animals in captivity is never ideal, but the fraught relationship between farmers and wildlife in sri lanka make it impossible for all elephants to live in the wild. perhaps in the future with better education, people all over the world will be better able to co-exist with animals and places like pinnewala will be unnecessary. however, for now this place is the best of a bad situation.

review_text_clean: we stopped off here on the way from kandy to negombo in time for the 2pm bath time. its the last thing we have done in sri lanka and has left a bitter taste. as this wasnt part of our planned itinerary, i did not do any research beforehand. wish i had. youll find plenty of articles which will dissuade you. the word orphanage is a well chosen one it fools you into thinking this might be ecotourism. there are no success stories about these elephants being released back to the wild, only a brag about how this is the largest herd of asian elephants handled by man. twice a day the elephants are walked across the road down to a river where masses of people crowd around taking selfies. one man sprays them from a water cannon. if they dont want to get wet, then tough. i watched several try to avoid the spray only to be herded back into its path with shouts and the bull hook. it is sad to see them just standing there not playing at all. it is not their choice to be at the river and they look unhappy. some of the handlers were interacting nicely with them, washing and scratching them. but others just sat on the rocks. i fail to see how the animals well-being is put first - a complete money making scheme 2500 rupees to watch at the riverside. in penance for participating in such unethical tourism i will be donating the cost of our tickets to save the elephants. im hopeful my review will deter at least a few people from visiting.
aspect_sentences: ['its the last thing we have done in sri lanka and has left a bitter taste.']

review_text_clean: i read a whole bunch of these reviews before we travelled to sri lanka. i really wanted to see the elephants and it was our honeymoon after all. we visited thailand last year and refused any elephant visits as they are so mistreated over there and we are very against elephant riding. our experience of pinnawala was delightfully reassuring and i felt relieved. the elephants are treated very well and no one was riding them or beating them with sticks - as some of these reviews suggest. they were free to walk around and were fed very generously. you can tell that all staff members look after them very well. yes - there some that have some chains around them. this is unfortunate but we asked why this was and didnt just assume. as this is an orphanage, a lot of these elephants wouldnt survive the wild because they are unwell or have certain illnesses. naturally, some are also a bit aggressive and therefore, to protect themselves and the other elephants they have some with chains. its the best of a bad situation for them but they are bathed separately and have the same amount of love and care as the others. the keepers also carry guide sticks to help direct the elephants to the bathing river etc. they never hit or hurt the elephants with these sticks, they just use them gently to guide them safely across the roads etc. i think the people here are doing an amazing thing and we loved seeing them. we didnt need to ride them or anything - it was just amazing to see them. what a wonderful place for them.
aspect_sentences: ['we visited thailand last year and refused any elephant visits as they are so mistreated over there and we are very against elephant riding.', 'the elephants are treated very well and no one was riding them or beating them with sticks - as some of these reviews suggest.']

review_text_clean: maybe the intentions of this orphanage were once good, they are definitely not now. this is a commercialized elephant breeding factory. most of the elephants are bred in the park, for the sole purpose of entertainment for tourists. caretakers are encouraging everyone to take photos and touch the elephants in exchange for tips. you can pay extra to feed a baby elephant, who is chained by itself in a cage surrounded by tourists. when we were there, the baby was freaking out, trying to get out of the chains and hurting herself. they get fed whenever a tourist pays, not only during feeding times. many elephants are chained up all day in the same spot. they get to go to the river 2 times a day you have seen the famous photos. even there many are chained up under water and caretakers push them underwater with a stick so they look like they are splashing around. many of them are showing signs of distress, rocking back and forth for hours at the time while being chained up. this does not happen in the wild. these compulsive movements cause life-threatening damage to the feet and joints of the elephant. they are in severe distress and dont let them tell you otherwise. people saying that there is no other way to treat them and the elephants would not survive in the wild are wrong. there are way more humane ways to treat elephants in an orphanage and this is not one of them. please dont participate.

review_text_clean: the first thing to note is the orphanage is more zoo like than i expected. i was also not really prepared to see some of the elephants chained to posts, however i also didnt expect one to walk past within ten feet of me either. the park is split into three sections - there is an area where you can feed fruit to an elephant, there is a holding area where the elephants are chained and fed and then there is a large paddock where they roam free. there are keepers who patrol the perimeter of the paddock, but other than a smattering of rocks, there is nothing between you and the elephants. whilst we were at the paddock, the elephant who had been at the fruit station, was walked back to the field in front of where we were stood. it was quite amazing. later on a group were walked down to the feeding station and again were no more than ten foot away from us. there is a daily milk feed for the orphans, and a walk down to the river for a bath, but on the day we were there, neither took place. unsure as to why the feeding didnt happen although i expect the babies would have been chained too not quite the romantic image i had, but the bathing was cancelled due to the rain causing river levels to be too high. would recommend as an opportunity to get close to the elephants, but not as one to view them in their natural habitat.
aspect_sentences: ['would recommend as an opportunity to get close to the elephants, but not as one to view them in their natural habitat.']

review_text_clean: so we had read so many mixed reviews and were debating whether to go or not. we decided to go and see for ourselves and make our own minds up in all honesty seeing these wonderful animals at such close proximity was amazing, would we prefer no chains - of course, but you can see in most cases it is for the elephant public safety as most do not have such chains when back in the ample enclosures. they seem to be well fed and love the water playing. bearing in mind that this place started with two elephants and takes in sick or injured as well as releases some back to the wild on balance they do a great job. seeing the keepers with hooked poles is not nice but we saw no ill treatment and more love than anything. cost for us foreigners is 2500 rupee around 12.50 each and bearing in mind that the money goes to help i see this as good value plus i paid 750 rupee for my wife to wash an elephant in the water - clearly enjoyed by the elephant and my wife. i do have issues with the elephants being ridden by the keepers also on the road into the orphanage a place offering ride an elephant service - this to me is totally wrong and should not be allowed! anyway in my humble opinion it was a wonderful experience

review_text_clean: we were taken to pinnawala elephant orphanage by our tour guide on our way to nuwara eliya from colombo. i had heard and read so much about this place that i definitely wanted to visit it. as soon as we entered we were pleased to see so many elephants in the river which was quite a sight. but after standing and looking at them for a bit, we realized that some of the elephants were chained up and forced to spray water from their trunks or were being forced to lie down. if they tried getting up the so called caretaker would pierce them with these long sharp and pionty spearrods in their hand. it made the the elephants scream loudcould be heard at a distance in pain and the care taker seemed to enjoy it. i really felt bad and we all decided to leave immediately. it dint feel as though the care taker had any kind of bond or cared even a bit for the elephants. i really hope that the government looks into it and hires people who actually want to do something for the elephants and not use them as props for tourism.

review_text_clean: this is a place that has many controversial reviews and so we pondered to whether we wanted to go or not. it was a tossup and i am glad we did go but it did leave some questions unanswered. we missed the elephants walking from the park over the road and down to the river. so we purchased our tickets from the ticket office and then headed over. you have to give your ticket to the ticket man at the start of the road so unpaid people cannot get down there to watch the elephants. we got down there and it was quite a sight. all these elephants standing in the water. the group of elephants was split and i did notice the ones that were chained in place. i also noted a small group that kept trying to get out of the water. the mahout would let them go for a while and then he would yell and wave his hook and the elephants obviously fearful of him would get back in the water. i got talking to another visitor who said she had been a number of times and that the river was really low and when it is low they seem to be lethargic. it was the first time she had seen them so disinterested. the mahout to me seemed to be a bully. later on when they were prepping them to leave, this particular guy caught my eye and smiled. i gestured to him that i was not happy with his behavior and proceeded to photograph him. i believe there is a difference to being in control fairly and being a bully. out of all of them he definitely was a bully. the elephants were swapped around a bit and it was fascinating to be so close and to watch them for a reasonably long period. it was extremely hot that day so we sat up in the restaurants balcony and had a beer etc. to get some respite. they then moved the elephants to the water cannon by the exit to the river which they seemed to enjoy and then the main girl elephant, she led them back up the road. they knocked over a hat stand in a store which was funny and they seemed keen to get back. we followed them closely and when we got back they had taken them over the back of the park and they were being fed. we stood for perhaps half an hour and no one told us what was happening- we just stood and hoped there was something more. eventually they told us we could go over which we did. yes they were all chained by a foot and they all had piles of food. we stood for a period watching how they ate soft wood, palm leaves and observed what they seemed to prefer to eat, and how they manipulated the food to eat. we then went back to another area where they had younger elephants still on milk. we got talking to the assistant curator and it wasnt until he answered my questions about containment, feeding, punishment, medical care, that it made any sense. he said there was a lot of misunderstanding and therefore there are negative reviews. i asked why they seemed to be not enjoying themselves in the water and he said, they are just so keen to get back to eat. the main reason for containment is to stop fighting. in the wild the elephants form packs where there is a boss and they will fight if they encroach on other elephants territory. they are working on a big open area for them but at the moment containment is the best for them. so this parks environment is not normal, but it is the best they can do and they do their best to stop the animals hurting each other. he said that the elephants do not have to work for their food there and life is quite easy and the care is excellent with medical care etc. and it is a good alternative for the orphans. i suggested they educate the visitors more. there was very little education of the visitors and when you dont know why things are being done, you come up with your own theory. the experience is not interactive enough. i also complained about the bully mahout and he knew who i was talking about and he has been pulled up before about this. i appreciate what this place is doing but think it is a shame that there are even orphans that need care. if they were just left to their own devices, and humans didnt interfere, there would be few orphaned anyway. i think they actually do really care for them and give them great care, but they need to connect with the visitors more and explain what and why and how they do what they do.

review_text_clean: we stayed at hotel elephant park. this is an excellent place to get up early, have breakfast and have some of the best seats in the house to a fantastic experience. photographs of the experience are readily available... the actual experience is way better. from the eyes of my 8 year old granddaughter, it was magical. you want to be done with breakfast by 830am when the first group of about 7 elephants come. you can move off the balcony of the hotel down to the rocks to get really close to the elephants, if you move down early you will beat the crowds and get pics you will treasure. once the elephants are guided away from the river, take an hour or so shopping the row of shops leading to the river. make sure you begin to make your way back toward the river just before 1000am. you will be able to see 40 elephants guide toward the river. you can stand within 2 feet or so of the procession. once safe, make your way back to the rocks by the water. this is an excellent vantage point to enjoy the spectacle. unfortunately i dont have anything positive to say about the actual orphanage. i imagine and believe that they are doing good work, but i cant personally vouch for it. we went before the 40 elephants were guided back to the orphanage, and i can say that within 10 min, the overwhelming impression my family got was depression. i would not recommend entrance to the elephant orphanage. enjoy the elephants while bathing. btw,if you are looking for an extremely high quality experience from a personal driver, i had an opportunity to work with both gamage asanka from gamage tours, gamagetours.com, i reached out to him because of a good review on trip advisor. from the first email, it was obvious he was responsive, quite courteous and professional. we began to work on an itinerary together, and received what i thought was very reasonable pricing for what i was asking him to do. when it came down describing our vehicle needs he was quick to note that since we had 4 people in our party, his vehicle would not be the best option. i appreciated his candor. he recommended a personal friend and colleague, gihan thissera, from sinethi tours, gihan took us on 7 review_text_clean: this was booked by our tour company for us. we did not therefore have to deal with getting tickets etc as our guide did all this for us and showed us were to go. first of all we went across the road from the main site towards the river where we watched the lephants bathing in the river. it was a lovely sight to see, i know some had chains on them but this we were informed was for safety reasons related to the behaviour of the specific elephant. the elephant hotel is an ideal spot to having a drnk and some lunch as they have a balcony area overlooking the river. we were fortunate to be browsing the shops down towards the river when the elephants were being brought back to the main sight. boy were they lively with a slight incident with one not behaving!!! back on the main sight we were able to see the elephants includiing a couple of tuskers we learnt that not all elephants have tusks. there is the chance to hand feed a elephant fruit which was 350 rupees and this was certainly memorable with the chance to touch them under the supervision of one of the keepers. there is also the chance to bottle feed a calf again under supervision - if youre going to flim or take pictures of this be quick they drain a large bottle of milk in the blink of an eye! it certainly was a bucket list exerience and lovely to see how they have taken them in for various reasons ad how well they are cared for.
aspect_sentences: ['the elephant hotel is an ideal spot to having a drnk and some lunch as they have a balcony area overlooking the river.']

review_text_clean: this place has something quite magical about it - the elephants of course. split across a road really it is a little bit complicated upon first arriving as you feel you shoud go into the actual orphanage but then a siren sounds and the elephants leave the grounds to cross the road, parade down a street full of shops ! and into the river but this is something you must see! its amazing to watch 40 elephants happy, frolic and even scrubbed by some of the orphanage workers. you can enjoy the view from a cafe or just from the pavement. proceed back up past the shops selling elephant dung toilet paper to the orphanage where you can enjoy feeding them or just watch them roam about in wide open spaces. some elephants are with chains which can be a little upsetting to initially see but it appears its only for those that are a bit unruly and could charge off. none are actually shackled to the ground although we did feel a bit taken advantage of by the river as a young elephant with a chain was used to pose for photos with tourists as workers pressed for money for each photo. try to avoid this if possible as you will have many opportunities to take photos of them in the river, on the road and in the orphanage without lining the pockets of opportunists using them for a photo opportunity. who wants a photo with chains in it anyway?

review_text_clean: we visited as a part of a day trip from negombo to kandy. we arrived early morning, at 0930 and were able to watch the baby elephants being bottle fed. you could also give it a go yourself if you asked. the elephants looked well treated and after walking around the orphanage, we were pleasantly surprised to be guided across the road by our tour guide to a local restaurant overlooking the rivers. the street was full of shops and people asking us to come in, which seemed decent if your into that kind of thing. we arrived at the restaurant and ordered some food western prices and after a few minutes, saw a huge herd 50 elephants coming down the streets into the large river to bathe. it was particular great to see they were completely free to play and wash no chains of ropes with a few of the handlers simply sat by on the rocks. absolutely fantastic to see and definitely recommended.

review_text_clean: having read some negative reviews on here about entrance fees and paying extra to feed the elephants i was pleasantly surprised to see the entrance fee clearly displayed on arrival. rd 2500 for foreigners and rs 100 for sri lankans and rs 700 for saarc nationals. twice daily you get the chance to bottle feed the babies or fruit feed the adults, who clearly love the attention they get. the elephants are kept in wonderful surroundings and are looked after very well. this is a tourist attraction but it has expanded to rescue elephants injured in the jungle and offer them a safe home for the rest of their lives with medical attention when needed. it is an amazing sight to see the elephants being led down to the river to bathe, some are tethered in the water, this is to protect the human visitors and also to stop the males harassing the females. there are a couple of hotelstea shops on the banks of the river from where you can sit and watch the elephants bathe and the road leasing from the river to the main park is lined with souvenir shops which are fun to browse. we thoroughly enjoyed our trip to the elephant orphanage, it is as close to seeing elephants in their natural environment as possible. i would recommend a visit, even for those who do not like to see animals in captivity, they are well kept and far better off here than in the places they were rescued from.

review_text_clean: i was a little unsure of how i felt about this place upon arrival. my driver dropped me off at the foreigner ticket booth where i paid maybe l35 usd for my ticket. when i went in there was a spot where people were paying to feed fruit to elephants. then an open area in the back were some elephants were just standing. it seemed like occasionally the staff were trying to corral the elephants closer to the tourists. i wasnt feeling great about the place. i walked down to see the milk feeding and again, people were paying to hold a bottle of milk for a single elephant in a caged in area while so many people made noise and took photos. it felt so commercial and unkind for the elephants. i left disheartened, not knowing that there was another area across the street where the elephants were taken to bath. my driver then showed me the area across the road, and for me this for me was magical. i watched maybe 30 elephants walk their usual path down to the river where a giant hose has been built to facilitate their bathing. ill admit, i was slightly distraught to see that some of the elephants had chains tied on their ankles that were then hung over their backs. they were not being led by chains and a near by sign explained that the chains are precautionary for the safety of the staff and tourists. i watched the elephants bath for almost an hour before deciding to have lunch at a restaurant that overlooked the bathing elephants. i did not once see the chains used. my only qualm is that some of the staff ride the elephants. i have heard that this is very bad for the elephants spines. i am no zoologist, and i welcome any additional info on the harm this may cause to the animals as i do not like to see animals being mistreated.

review_text_clean: we visited the orphanage on the way round to dambulla. we had read reviews on tripadvisor but we were undecided whether to visit. in the end we felt that perhaps our entrance fee would contribute to the elephant upkeep so we proceeded to visit. on arrival and purchase of tickets we were taken down a small shopping street opposite to the orphanage which takes you to the river where the elephants bathe daily. we arrived to see at least 30 elephants enjoying the water with some snorkelling and a couple of younger ones being a little cheeky. this part of the visit was great. we did not wait to see all the elephants make their way back past the shops and street stalls but that might have been fun. back at the orphanage the pens, albeit large, just did not offer any stimulation for the elephants. even though they are trying to make improvements the orphanage itself was not what we expected or would like to consider as acceptable for keeping what are wild elephants. we were saddened by what we saw and it left us thinking why not take them to one of the national parks and releasing them back to the wild. probably not that simple but thats how it left us feeling.
aspect_sentences: ['this part of the visit was great.']

review_text_clean: we visited pinnawala elephant orphanage on our way to kandy from colombo. initially i did not have high hopes of seeing anything extraordinary. after entering we had to walk for some distance in the hot sun seeing only one or two elephants chained inside their enclosure. but at the end of our walk, we were treated to a fascinating sight of more than 50 elephants roaming about in an open area enclosed by rocks and railings to prevent them from coming out. then we watched some elephants being fed and some people were allowed to feed milk to baby elephants in bottles. after coming out, we were told that the elephants would come out, cross the road, walk into the street and take a bath in the river. we waited outside for some time and then the gates opened and more than 30 elephants came out, crossed the road and walked into the street within 5 feet of where we were standing. it is both awesome and scary to have 25 elephants walking right next to you, trumpeting and swaying and one elephant swerved dangerously close to where i was standing. after they crossed us, we followed them to the river by paying the charges and were again treated to a rare sight of so many elephants bathing together in the river. all in all, it was a wonderful and unforgettable experience and i am very happy that i paid a visit to this place. i have no hesitation in recommending this attraction to all of you who are visiting sri lanka.
