review_text_clean: honestly. i thought i would write something that will help guide your decision about whether to go or not, however it isnt straight up and simple. ive tried to bullet point my thoughts to try and help. 1. yes there are chains on some elephants. i believe some have shown aggressive behaviours. there are some very not well looked after elephants in extremely worse situations i have seen across the island. 2. the milk feed i am in two minds about. it is done to obviously provide money for the elephants. the two we saw were not in shackles, were boisterously playing around the site and seemed more than happy to keep drinking away, and were more teenager-ish stature. 3. the river. they seemed more than happy to splash about in the river. some elephants were having their keepers wash them, one elephant didnt want him to stop, encouraging him when he stopped until he carried on again. two elephants were chained on a long chain, they had enough room to play and their keepers could leave them safely there. it didnt seem any different to when you nip into the corner shop with your dog tied by its lead to the lamppost outside. 4. i did see one keeper prodding an elephant with a sharp pointed spear type implement at one point when it appeared to be going off track. this concerned me a little, however no elephant i had a good look at had any wounds, there were happy calves with their mums. they kept the bulls separate to the rest of the herd as they generally get territorial and violent. if you do not like zoos, do not go. minneriya national park is nearby and has wild herds.
aspect_sentences: ['minneriya national park is nearby and has wild herds.']

review_text_clean: after some initial concerns, we decided to visit pinnawala orphanage and we enjoyed it yet it did raise some concerns. the ticket for locals is a bargain. foreigners pay much more, but i guess you need to maintain such a place and its be unfair to overcharge locals. the place is indeed huge, beautiful and well-kept. its all surrounded by the jungle. the orphanage enclosure is all done with wood and trunks and there is varied and typical vegetation there are signs for the trees. the fruit feeding of adult elephants and milk feeding of the young ones has a little of a show feeling, but if you try paying a somehow reasonable price, youll get the chance to have a unique experience, get close to the elephants and touch them. the unruly young ones were cute and insatiable. the adults seemed to enjoy the fruit and none seemed to be forced to eat. across the place there are lots of signs with information about elephants and their care and feeding. in a world where human beings are taking space from the wildness to build towns and roads, pinnawale has a caring aim. seeing a few unruly young ones chained was cause of concern, yet i want to believe thats the only option to keep the most unruly ones and that at some point, they are unchained and allowed to be in other open areas. its a different experience from a zoo and a from a circus. i have heard otherwise yet i dont have those strong opinions. these elephants were separated by their own herds so at least they appear to be looked after and they may not have had many chances out there alone.

review_text_clean: my mother and i visited here on our holiday to srilanka. i last visited 15 years ago. the elephants have their own section of never ending land to roam around. large boulders are in place so the public do not enter. i loved that now these beautiful animals have their own space rather than being bombarded with people around them. they walk down to the river through shops to bath. its truly fantastic to see. yes the elephants are chained though which is hugely sad i believe its one leg. you cannot go into the river with the elephants which is also a nice touch i think as they have their own time to wash and do their own thing rather than pose with humans in the river.

review_text_clean: came here with my partner and our three youngest. firstly, it was enlightening to read the information at the entrance regarding the welfare of the animals, apart from which they had such vast grounds to roam in and the wonderful river to bathe in. we only saw two elephants with chains on their ankles, but the reason for this was explained - apart from this all the elephants seemed well cared for and had plenty of freedom. watching them frolicking in the river was awesome and provided excellent photo opportunities. we then all had to stand back whilst they walked back up the road the the other area. we spent ages in awe just watching them walking around and the babies playing and then moved on to the feeding area. we were too late to purchase a milk bottle, but, that being said we were able to purchase some fruit to feed to them - what an amazing experience for the children. i firmly believe that this orphanage works to help elephants and i am unsure as to why some people have a different view. a wonderful day was had by all!
aspect_sentences: ['we only saw two elephants with chains on their ankles, but the reason for this was explained - apart from this all the elephants seemed well cared for and had plenty of freedom.']

review_text_clean: ultimately good. we hiked through the forest and reached the upper and lower diyaluma falls. there is a natural pool. when we went the water was more. our guide helped us to find a safe place to have a bath. he took us with passion and patience . his name is upendra. he speaks and understand english. we parked our car near the village . from there along with tuktuk to go up and down until the hiking point. he also came with us until the falls. he can be contacted at 0775474725. our driver got a good deal by talking with him for both tuktuk and being a guide. after bath we changed our wet clothes in his house. friendly people. i have included his photo with his shop. the falls and the forest just got imprinted into our heart. beautiful road to the falls and extraordinary hike upto the top of the falls. a must do. but people should restrain from polluting the place with plastics.
aspect_sentences: ['friendly people.']

review_text_clean: this was one of our favourite days in sri lanka. definitely worth a visit. as others say below, you can go with or without a guide. we had a guide from ella whose company we really enjoyed, so we went up with him but you could definitely find your way without a guide if you wanted to, maybe with a wrong turn or two along the way. we took the short 20-minute walk rather than the 2-hour hike, and didnt regret it. the bottom pool is the busiest with tourists but we found it was only really worth a short stay. the views are beautiful, and this is where everyone gets their photos but thats pretty much it. the second pool, a very short walk away, is good for a swim, and the view of the falls above you is pretty special. the third pool, directly above the second, and a short 2-3 minute hike up, features an 8m cliff jump. we did it and were perfectly safe but i wouldnt do it without being shown by a local guide. there are plenty around the first pool who can show you. we did it a couple of times every time, my feet hit the bottom of the pool at the end of the jump, but not hard enough to be of any concern just a surprise first time around! we then had a lovely time at the top of the third pool, sitting in the sun and relaxing. well worth a trip.
aspect_sentences: ['the third pool, directly above the second, and a short 2-3 minute hike up, features an 8m cliff jump.']

review_text_clean: stunning multiple waterfalls and a great place to swim. guides are not needed !! after thoroughly researching the falls we were confident on how to get to them with clear instructions saved on our phones. after parking our tuk tuk at the top carpark we were asked multiple times if we would like a guide. after saying no and following our saved directions we set off to find our path only to be followed by one of the guides from the carpark. we were told we were going the wrong way and he directed us down some path in which he said was the right way. we trusted this advice as we thought he was being genuinely helpful. this path was overgrown and full of leeches have a bottle of insect repellent and lighter ready to sprayburn them off as soon as you feel them after eventually reaching and exploring the waterfalls we found a much much better path back. we popped out surprise, surprise where we were originally headed before being led astray by the guides advice. after returning to our tuk tuk and confronting the guide we asked him if the path we were going to follow was were the guides go and he laughed in our face and said yes. we expressed our disappointment at his actions and said in australia or new zealand we would never do this to tourists or deliberately lead them astray simply because they chose to make their own way. below are clear instructions how to get the falls without utilising the guides who take advantage of tourists and deliberately confuse them or make up that google maps wont work or that its extremely difficult to find the falls, both of which turned out to be lies. follow this reviews instructions - however after walking past the green and white gate walk for about 50m then take a sharp right onto a wide path. from there traverse around the hillside towards the sound of rushing water and youll find the various waterfalls.
aspect_sentences: ['stunning multiple waterfalls and a great place to swim.']

review_text_clean: we are a family of 4 2 kids age 1013 and spent the day around the falls. we took a bus from ella to wellawaya 45 min, 300 rs. from there, our guide for the day tharindu, 94 719702456 picked us up by tuktuk. of you have a car, you could also come straight to the falls on your own. tharindu lives at the base of the falls. we first spent half and hour climbing and playing on the boulders at the bottom of the fallsriver. then tharindu brought us with the tuktuk halfway up the mountain, from where we hiked 30 min to the falls. we recommend bringing a guide, because it saves you a lot of walking and you wont get lost which is easy. when we got to the top of the falls, it was a bit crowded with locals because of the weekend. we hiked 10 min further up to upper diyaluma falls, which where even nicer! there, we swam in the pools and climbed up to the top, from where our kids jumped off from a 8 meter rock in the pool! awesome! tharindu was really nice and helpful and encouraged the kids with the swimming and jumping. he also makes really nice pictures and loves the panorama setting!. we had a great day all together. dont hesitate to give tharindu a call.
aspect_sentences: ['we had a great day all together.']

review_text_clean: diyaluma falls is the second highest waterfall in sri lanka at 720ft high. located about 6km from koslanda in the badulla district, and 38km from ella, this horsetail waterfall has multiple falls and natural pools for you to dive into, refresh yourself and explore. diyaluma falls can be explored from both above and below, as the base of the falls also has a pool you can dive into! the best time to visit would be for sunrise as you get to see the rising sun shine upon the waves crashing down, however, sunset isnt a bad option either, just be weary that you may need to travel back towards the main road in total darkness.

review_text_clean: thia waterfall is amazing ! first, the hike to the uppermost level of the waterfall takes you through breathtaking scenery. mind that you have to do proper research online so you find out the right way for the beautiful hike. the starting point is a fee hundred meters south from diyaluma falls inn. the local tuk tuk drivers will try to sell you tours, no need to get one. once you get to the top of the waterfall, you start to descend, following the flow of water and you go through several stages of the waterfall, each with beautiful little pools where you can take baths. the lowest level is actually the top of the waterfall that you see from the main road. from there, you descend on a dirt path and reach a point close to naulla village. so, the start and end points are different. this is the best way to go, in my opinion. you will enjoy amazing views and a good workout

review_text_clean: i gave it 4 stars because of the tough climb to get to the top. otherwise, it is indeed a multi-level beautiful waterfall with a number of pools to sit or have fun in. we rode a motorbike from ella, took about 1-1.5hrs. fairly good roads except for the last 15min stretch which were bumpier. at the base of the waterfall some distance away from the actual waterfall, there is a small parking area and an inn. there are a few local boys young men waiting and will offer their service as a guide. we could have bargained to 1500lkr but paid the 2000lkr asked, after hearing from other travellers at our guesthouse how they topped up 500lkr in the end after experiencing the amount of walking and the guide waiting to bring them down at the end. the walk up starts with a fairly straightforward dirt path through rubber trees and a small cluster of houses. however, the rest of it is a climb up the mountain, on uneven, scrabbly rocks, large and small, and cut-in steps in the ground. you should be young or of moderate fitness to do this. definitely wear proper shoes and have sunscreen and water. preferably start early in the day and wear longer pants, as the tall grass growing towards the path for much of the climb can get itchy after a while. you will also appreciate the helping hand of the guide as you climb.. at the top there is a coconut seller, then slightly downhill to the actual waterfall. it is fairly easy to get to the various levels of the waterfall. be careful stepping in and out of the pools as the rocks are slippery with moss. there is only a roti and coconut seller at the waterfall itself. bring some snacks or you can buy them from the few village grocery shops on the road in. very friendly locals, we smiled and waved to everyone. from the bottom of the waterfall, you will need to climb back up again to the top where the coconut seller is, to go all the way down again. it takes about 1hr each way.
aspect_sentences: ['there are a few local boys young men waiting and will offer their service as a guide.', 'be careful stepping in and out of the pools as the rocks are slippery with moss.', 'very friendly locals, we smiled and waved to everyone.']

review_text_clean: we visited here on the advice of our guesthouse in haputale. we hiked up and down liptons seat in the morning and then caught the wellawaya bus at about 2pm. bus was mega full it was a sunday and we didnt get a seat. it was hot and bumpy and we were happy to get of the bus after 1hr and a half. it was dry season so there wasnt much water, but the falls were impressive nonetheless. we didnt hang around too long at the bottom because it was a bit touristy. instead we attempted the hike to the top, as described in the lonely planet 2012 edition. a young boy from the village volunteered to guide us along the way. to be honest we would have struggled without him, so we gave him 10rs. ostensibly to buy school supplies. he put us on the right path and we scrambled up for 20min to the top. you should make sure to take plenty of water for the hike, and dont wear flip-flops. at the top we hoped to have the pools to ourselves, as we were hot and sweaty and just wanted to jump in the water. surprisingly there were a few groups of locals one getting a bit boozy, and some german girls attracting attention in their bikinis. we just took our boots off and cooled our feet off while chatting to the locals apparently a family of wild elephants come here for a drink most days at around 630pm. sadly we didnt go to the top of the actual falls, because we had to get the bus back to haputale. it looked really cool and would probably make a great photo. the real highlight for me was in fact the bus ride back up to haputale. buses going up come approx. every 30min, and the last one is at 1830. it took us just over an hour to hike up, 20min at the top, and 45min to get back down, so we caught the bus at about 1720. there was plenty of space on the bus, and it was a magical journey through the forested hills overlooking the southern lowlands as the sun sets over the mountains. keep your eyes peeled for macaques as you drive up! give yourself more time than we did if youre using public transport. alternatively, if you have your own transport, take a torch with you, stay to see the elephants.

review_text_clean: its about an easy 30 minute trail path walk from the car park. directions facing the car park take the road left and follow it bearing right around the corner. after about 5 minutes you will come across and green and white gate looks like private property drive going downhill. go through the gate, or if its locked you can walk around it. a few metres in front is a sign and take the path that leads right. its a clear footpath the whole way and it leads through a field of long grass, not very steep. follow this trail for about 1520 minutes and you will hear the waterfall. you will see a hut and follow the path to the right a few hundred metres. you will see the pools and the rest is pretty simple from there! be careful the big rock you have to walk across is quite steep, some people were sliding down on their bums. its totally worth it even just to swim around the upper pools, they are beautiful. some points you can jump off ledges into, theyre very deep. the sri lankan children are dare devils and very fun to watch. we didnt go down to the actual waterfall because we didnt have time, our taxi driver gave us 2 hours. but could have easily spent half a day here.

review_text_clean: i and my family had a thoroughly enjoyable trip to this 170 m high waterfall . it is about 14 km from the hilly town of haputale. the view moving out of the this town is captivating as it is situated on a ridge . the bus trip from haputale to the diyaluma falls takes 45 minutes., going towards welawaya. the falls is situated by the roadside with sprays falling onto the road . we took a walk thru the rubber plantation with many village homes enroute. there is a few paths leading up but one can always ask the village folks. a young boy of 12 years became our guide and he is really well informed and fun to be with. we walked up through temperate shrub land for about 45 minutes with many stops along the way to enjoy the views . at the top it was pristine and gives a top of the world feeling looking down at the massive falls below. many small falls are scattered around and provided much fun for my teenage childrem. one can choose to explore further inland following the river but it was too tiring. there are villagers selling coconuts and food at the bottom of the falls.

review_text_clean: seeing the bodi tree and temple complex was really interesting. this was the start of our tour of the cultural triangle and it makes a great place to start. our driver suggested a guide which we took for 2000r and it was well worth it to understand the symbolism and rituals s week as the history which you can get from any guidebook. understanding the moon and guardstones for example set us up for appreciating all the other temples we saw and was a good starting point for our kids aged 13 and 10. the site is super busy with tourists but also regular worshippers and thats what made it so interesting compared with other less busy temples. stay and watch the processions and you will learn about localreligious customs. on a practical note as its so hot and you need to remove your shoes, kids and sometimes adults can wear socks so bring a pair with. you need to cover shoulders and below the knee so having a sarong in your bag is very handy if you dont want to wear trousers. you cant wear hats or caps either.
aspect_sentences: ['this was the start of our tour of the cultural triangle and it makes a great place to start.']

review_text_clean: jaya sri maha bodhi is the most sacred place in anuradhapura. it is a raised platform in mahameghawana gardens which contains a branch of a fig tree called maha bodhi in buddhism under which mahatma buddha is stated to have attained enlightenment nirwan in buddha gaya, india. this tree sapling was planted here in 249 bc and is known as the oldest surviving tree in the world which has a known date of plantation. it was brought here by sangamitta, daughter of emperor ashoka of india with great pomp and show 2500 years ago. emperor ashoka was himself present in the celebrations held at the indian port of tamalitta in which this sapling was dispatched to sri lanka in a ship. sri lankan king devanam piyatissa himself received the sapling at the sri lankan port with great honor and pageantry. while standing under this tree, i thought that it was like a peepel tree. for about two billion people of the world, it is the most sacred tree and is called roots of paradise on earth by buddhists.

review_text_clean: one of the worlds oldest recorded trees and certainly the most revered, visited by buddhists from all around the world. it is said to have grown from a cutting of the original tree under which the buddha attained enlightenment in india. the tree has been tended for 23 centuries and cuttings have been taken and planted in temples throughout the island. there is no entrance charge as far as we could tell but security here is tighter than at other attractions in sri lanka a result of the bombings in 1998 and there separate lines for men and women. this is a sacred place so, as for all temples, you must dress respectfully legs and shoulders covered. you need to remove hats and shoes. you are allowed to keep socks on and i would recommend this as it is a bit of a walk to get to the tree at the centre of the complex. the site was very tranquil and it was interesting to visit for the history. you need to bear in mind that you will not be able to get a close up view of the tree as it is enclosed by a wall and railings. only two branches of the original tree remain, and these are supported by props. this is the main reason we personally didnt feel able to score higher than a 3. devotees on a pilgrimage will obviously feel very differently.

hatton. anuradhapura is one of the ancient capitals of sri lanka, world famous for its well preserved ruins of the great sri lankan civilization. the civilization which was built upon this city was one of the greatest civilizations of asia and in the world. the city is now a unesco heritage site. today this ancient city of sri lanka, which is sacred to the buddhist world, and which its anuradhapura, including thuparamaya where the collarbone of buddha is enshrined, isurumuniyaa picturesque rock temple and the sacred jaya siri maha bodhi at mahaviharaya mahameghavana park which is recorded as the oldest surviving historical tree in the world, i took a bus back to colombo from anuradhapura new town at 1pm. the oldest surviving tree in the world, the sacred jaya siri maha bodhi large and very old sacred fig tree ficus religiosa located in bodh gaya about 100 km 62 mi from patna in the indian state of bihar, under which siddhartha gautama, the spiritual teacher later known as eyes, gazing at it with gratitude. the term bodhi tree is also widely applied to currently existing trees, including the bodhi tree in anuradhapura, sri lanka, which has a great significance in the history of buddhism. this bodhi tree in anuradhapura is widely mentioned in mahavamsa. while not considered a canonical religious text, the mahavamsa is an important text in theravada buddhism. it covers the early history of religion in sri lanka, beginning with the time of siddhartha gautama, the founder of buddhism. according to the mahavamsa, the sri maha bodhi in sri lanka was planted in 288 bc, making it the oldest verified specimen of any angiosperm. in this year the twelfth year of king asokas reign the right branch of the bodhi tree was brought by sanghamitt? to anur?dhapura and placed by dev?n?mpiyatissa his left foot in the mah?meghavana. the buddha, on his death bed, had resolved five things, one being that the branch which should be taken to ceylon should detach itself. from gay?, the branch was taken to p?taliputta, thence to t?malitt?, where it was placed in a ship and taken to jambukola, across the sea finally it arrived at anuradhapura, staying on the way at tivakka. those who assisted the king at the ceremony of the planting of the tree were the nobles of k?jarag?ma and of candanag?ma and of tivakka. according to the mahavamsa, branches from the bodhi trees of all the buddhas born during this kalpa were planted in ceylon sri lanka on the spot where the sacred bodhi tree stands today in anur?dhapura. later, after completing my visit to the other attractions of the ancient ruins holy city of anuradhapura i took a bus back to colombo from anuradhapura new town at 1pm and reached the pettah bus station in colombo at 8pm to put-up a night at a nearby low cost lodge, i.e. classic inn in panchikawatte road before leaving for the bandaranaike airport at 6am of 1511 to catch the 12.55pm flight back to malaysia.

review_text_clean: the surrounding grounds and trees make this an interesting cultural place to visit .. you really need to understand the meaning of religion to buddhists to appreciate the peace that comes to the followers .. the tree as described is the oldest anywhere, but worth taking a look it .. the temple itself probably looked much grander in its earlier days but historically has meaning .. statues around the area are visible for all to see .. i didnt have a guide to pass me any information but still enjoyed wandering around .. as everywhere else around sri lanka monkeys run freely, and might try to grab your bags .. dont carry any food or they will chase you, otherwise will just leave you alone .. its also pretty hot and you will have to walk around barefoot so wear socks to keep your feet protected from the ground ..

review_text_clean: let me create a laundry list of pros and cons explaining my poor rating pros the surrounding park area is nice and relatively peaceful, filled with monkeys and chirping birds. cons - touts, touts, touts. as is endemic throughout sri lanka, you find yourself having to stave off wannabe tour guides, and overly aggressive park attendants. there was a place left to deposit shoes before entering the holy site, with no sign mentioning a fee. within seconds of leaving, i was aggressively hounded for a full 5 minutes by a tout demanding a ridiculous donation or fee for leaving my shoes outside. when i politely declined, he left for a moment, then returned to demand a 100 rupee note. i politely explained that i had paid thousands of rupees to enter the park and grounds itself an exorbitant 3125 rupees and that i wasnt in the mood to deposit 100 rupee notes in each and every site i visited, or to every tout who crossed my path - i would have easily been short another 2000 rupees for that day alone. i ended up, perhaps immaturely, offering a small handful of 2 rupee coins. he eventually backed off. this collection of experiences ruined what should have otherwise been a peaceful visit.
aspect_sentences: ['let me create a laundry list of pros and cons explaining my poor rating pros the surrounding park area is nice and relatively peaceful, filled with monkeys and chirping birds.']

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text_clean: our guide took us in the evening to see the great buddha tooth - we queued for over 30mins in the heat no ac inside and lots of people with people trying to push infront of us! when finally the awful loud procession music stopped, the queue moved forward to see the tooth - except is behind about 2 distance walls of glass and youre not allowed to stop so i had no idea what i was looking at, honestly comical. and locals leave offering to the buddha tooth that the monks love im sure. the temple itself is lovely, lots of detail, nice paintings but dont go with the crowds in the evening its not worth it. enjoy it at a quieter time to take it all in. note - there is a place to store shoes outside as you have to take them off so pack socks as the floor is dirty theres also a weird room with a huge stuffed elephant that the president or someone loved. after going to the elephant freedom project sanctuary earlier in the week highly recommend it felt cruel he had this as a pet in his garden.
aspect_sentences: ['our guide took us in the evening to see the great buddha tooth - we queued for over 30mins in the heat no ac inside and lots of people with people trying to push infront of us!']

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text_clean: if you are not a religious person that understands where to go, when and whats happening there at that moment, you wont enjoy the place much, neither the ceremony that happens at the place when its open to the public. not to mention that the place is a maze and it took me and my boyfriend some time to get to the entrance that we needed. different prices for locals and for tourists are present also here, as everywhere else at sri lanka. the ceremony is a mass activity where a lot of people pushes themselves to a certain place at the temple, and you push yourself to get there also, since you dont know why are others pushing themselves so much. the fact it, the religious people want to give their offerings to the temple and to buddha. you will end up in a room where everyone is packed, waiting to get to the room for offerings, where you wont get. so since you know about this now, you dont need to push yourself together with them and i have just saved you some time and nerves. instead of pushing yourself with the mass, i recommend you to walk around the temple and the parts that are accessible for the visitors, and e.g. burn some candles as your offering outside. the place looks magical, especially in the evening when its already dark outside. to burn something, you need to buy a special oil for that. i didnt figure out where to do that, unfortunately. what got me was a payment payment machine looking as an atm that could be used for donations for the temple. like wow. a way to go, the temple of the sacred tooth relic! this is what i call progress.
aspect_sentences: ['different prices for locals and for tourists are present also here, as everywhere else at sri lanka.']

review_text_clean: we joined the queues during morning prayer. there are two queues to get in one for the men and one for the women. like most things in life, the mens line moved faster. this is mainly due to two things 1 most women carry bags that need searching most men dont 2 the women perhaps face a little more scrutiny over what they can wear and must cover-up. shoulders and legs need to be covered, so make sure you have a light scarf and sarong. men too should carry a sarong to put on although some western males it seemed were managing to get through in shorts. once inside make sure you follow the tourist crowds to the right and enter the temple through the tourist entry. here you leave your shoes, you will be expected to tip after collection. inside, at prayer, this place is busy. at times you are moved along with the crowd. the locals are of course queuing to leave gifts and to pray so dont feel too bad if you skip queues and glide past those locals waiting on the stairs. the relic itself cant be seen. instead, you can peer into the golden shrine where it is stored, but at this point in the temple, the crowds are at their busiest so you main only manage a cursory glance. the best part about the temple is exploring the grounds and additional rooms and buildings. the carvings and sculptures of budha are beautiful, and in most spaces, you can take photos. just be mindful of people worshipping and not to take pictures with your back to any budha statue. the grounds of the temple are beautiful, and there is an elephant on the site too, which is used in ceremonies. although, it is clearly an old elephant and seeing it so heavily chained doesnt make for the best view. at night time, around the temple and lake, there is a cacophony of noise as bats and birds come to roost in their hundreds. it is the most spectacular site in kandy and a must-see. the museum of world buddhism, which is on the site is also worth a visit, and with a tourist ticket to the temple, you have access.
aspect_sentences: ['the museum of world buddhism, which is on the site is also worth a visit, and with a tourist ticket to the temple, you have access.']

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text_clean: this is another unesco world heritage site with interesting history and background. the site is located in city centre of kandy right in front of kandy lake. tooth relic is believed to be sacred for buddhism and the royal family was responsible for the safekeeping of the tooth relic. it is believed to be brought from anuradhapura to kandy kingdom. two storeys building was constructed for safekeeping the tooth relic. but the building was destroyed several times. each time it was restored whenever it was destroyed. there will be ceremony everyday for the blessings by the devotees. we visited around late afternoon and waited for the ceremony around 6pm plus. interesting cultural sights, but be prepared for uncontrollable crowds and haphazard situation during the ceremony. the tooth relic is said to be kept within a gold plated ornament, hence it cannot be seen by anyone even during the ceremony. the international buddhism museum within the compound is worth to check out too for the interesting architecture and interior design. overall, it is still worth the entrance fee of lkr1,500 per person and appropriate attire is required and tight security check at the entrance.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text_clean: we are a couple in early 30s with 9 and 10yr old daughters. firstly we hadnt dressed appropriately so had to rent sarongs to cover up. the guy was nice enough but still 400rs down. its a bit of a faff to get in, we went through one lot if security then you get your bag checked again before you go in. we had a tip off from the sarong guy that they take away your cigarettes and lighters so i hid them well in the bag. you have to put your shoes in a shoe storage area. other reviews are correct about them asking for a donation, i was aware of this and just played deaf when they asked me, i had to assist my child... oh and dont think you can put your shoes in your bag - thats not allowed! the ticket machines dont give change so you do have to have the right amount on you. there was an attendant who said we didnt have to pay for the children which was good and we didnt have the right change but he helped a guy behind us which then gave us the right change. so that was kind. first off you walk on boiling hot pavement in bear feet. then i guess the rest is interesting if you like architecture and religious history. as atheists we were a little bemused by all of it. theres nothing to tell you where the tooth is. we assumed we were in the right place by the people praying on the floor... but theres no signs etc and we didnt have a guide. theres a museum which was a little interesting. the saddest part is the taxidermied elephant. poor thing was captured and kept for a good 50years before he died. hes now stuffed in a glass cabinet. theres a photo timeline of his life since capture but it doesnt have any translation so we dont really know the story... if you like this sort if thing and are in kandy then maybe pay it a visit... but i definitely wouldnt drive to kandy for a day trip just for that. in my husbands words i wouldnt go again even if it was outside my front door.
aspect_sentences: ['first off you walk on boiling hot pavement in bear feet.']

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text_clean: get your information and timing right if you wish to visit this ancient and holy place. the door to the main relic is opened at specific timings, so check before you plan your trip. while the doors to the main shrine are closed, the crowds start building up, so if crowds scare you this place is an absolute no. although the crowds are quite well behaved. be sure to cover your shoulders and legs else shell out money to locals for giving you wraps etc. you need to buy tickets at the entrance from kiosks which need exact change. you will need to remove and deposit shoes at the counters outside. once inside it gives you the feel of an ancient place but well preserved and maintained. lots of devotees with offerings throng the temple every day. do not miss the oil lamps lighted outside by numerous devotees. you are allowed to take pictures but take care not to have your back towards the main shrine - else you will be asked to delete them by the vigilant guards. you marvel at the architecture of the temple and palace and leaves you asking fir more. the gardens are huge and well kept. i would recommend going there in the evenings, and once the temple visit is done you can enjoy the beauty of the kandy lake and the hills in the background.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text_clean: we saw that the temple of the sacred tooth relic was on every list when we researched things to do in kandy. it is, of course, a beautiful temple. i especially liked the ceiling murals near the main entrance. the main temple, however, was so crowded that it was hard to enjoy. we happened to be there near the new year, when many people were coming with offerings. you will need to leave your shoes at one of two kiosks before entering the temple. therefore, the walk from the shoe kiosk to the temple can be uncomfortably hot on your feet, so plan accordingly and perhaps wear socks. also, there are ticket machines where you buy your tickets, and for some reason they require exact change. very bizarre. there is a man sitting near the machines who will give you change, but it was an odd encounter because we didnt really know who he was or what he was doing. overall, i was underwhelmed and went because it is so famous. however, i feel our visit to kandy could have been fine without this.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text_clean: the sacred temple of tooth relic is located right in d centre of kandy city. there are multiple entrances and we made d mistake of entering from d main entrance. we literally stood for a good half hour to clear security. its too crowded. after entering inside we realised theres other not so crowded entrances too. entry for foreigners is 1000lkr. its a huge temple complex. the actual tooth relic is open to public only twice a day. we werent tht lucky to see it. there are also a couple of museums inside d complex,do check them out. spend some time exploring d whole complex. click a lot of pics. if ur in kandy then do visit this temple that holds the actual tooth of lord buddha. whole temple had peaceful positive vibes. we especially enjoyed the visit to the buddhism in the world museum,u will easily miss it in d premises if u dont go looking for it. do visit it, the entrance ticket includes d entry for d museum. it has some unbelievably amazing exhibits

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text_clean: the temple of the sacred tooth holds sri lankas most sacred relic, a tooth of the buddha. unfortunately we did not get to see the casket housing the relic, but were still awed by the beauty of the architecture and the dcor of the frescoes, moonstones and wooden frames. see the beautiful seated statue of a golden buddha flanked by two white marble statues, other images and the ivory tusks, and then look to the ornamentation of the ceiling above. the main hall showcases man statue of the buddha in various poses suspended plaques over each give an explanation of he painted scene above. at ceiling height, above each statue, there is a sculpture of an elephant head and tusks, all coloured gold. some wonderful features both indoors and to the buildings exteriors. the complex was crowed with tourists and worshippers, sound muted as if all acknowledge the sanctity of the place.

review_text_clean: this is the place where they house the tooth of the the great gautam buddha. points to note 1. pl wear at least knee length clothes to respect the area and the concept. 2. avoid visiting during peak noon hours as the distance between the shoe stand and the covered temple premise is a long one and you may get discomfort due to the heated stoned pathway. 3. take a guide and as k him not to hurry. 4. do not take snaps with the idols in the background. it is considered as a mark of disrespect. my experience for a guide was not very great. so, will not dwell in this issue much. the entry fees is less for saarc country members, so pl use the correct machine. the machine is automated well enough to provide you with the tickets. the casket - made of gold and the tooth is protects is not open throughout the year. so, check your visit date and expect accordingly. there is a museum within this premises and it is heart touching enough to see how well they have created the various blocks of all countries where buddhism is or was prevalent. date of experience march 2019.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text_clean: considered as a sacred temple complex containing the sacred tooth relic of lord buddha, shri dalada maligawa also known as palace of sacred tooth. this temple is a must visit for every buddhist. the tooth relic was originally housed in a rock carved temple in anuradha pura before it was moved to the present palace temple at kandy about five hundred years ago. this centuries old temple is serene and the worshippers pray in silence. the temple was originally built as a royal residential palace by the royal family of sri lanka long time ago. the remarkable features of this temple is the renowned recital of kandy drums is a joy to hear. the musical performance is unique for sri lanka.the musical instruments are two drums and a pipe instrument. the performance lasting about half an hour is precisely choreographed. the puja timings are fixed lasting about half an hour three times in a day - morning, noon and evening. the temple premises are very well secured and spotless maintenance is visible everywhere. you need to be properly dressed to enter the temple. ensure that your shoulder and knees are covered. the temple management treats every body equal. no preference seems to be given for any one. there is no shouting at or pushing of the pilgrims in the sanctum sanctorium. everything is done in dignified silence. the temple is a must visit while you are in kandy, sri lanka. highly recommended.
aspect_sentences: ['the remarkable features of this temple is the renowned recital of kandy drums is a joy to hear.', 'the temple management treats every body equal.']

review_text_clean: overhyped and overpriced tourist attractiontemple that doesnt seem to have much of an atmosphere or pays respect to a religion. its starts with paying the entrance fee, which basically feels like sponsoring the government. after dropping your shoes you enter the temple and dont really know what a logical way is to start, especially since its super crowded. we went for the ceremony but all it really was, was some guys banging a drum really loud for more then an hour. while that happend on the first floor on the second floor a queue of people pushing each other around formed to look in to a window for not even a second which apparently showed something important. im still not sure what it was. the temple has some pretty aspects but they mainly show in the hallways in the form of patterns and wallpaintings. after your whole experience youll go and pick up your shoes and get to deal with the guys behind the desk forcing you to put money in a donation box while clinching on to your shoes. kind of defeats the purpose of a donation doesnt it?

review_text_clean: we visited the temple with our guide - the best way to have the inside knowledge. we went to see the offerings at 9.30am, at this time some separate rooms are opened which arent usually open during other hours. fyi you cant actually see the tooth it is well protected in a stupa which is behind a closed door but open during the offering time. it was quite busy but use your manners and getting around is fine. as it is a sacred place, clothing is more strict. leggings for women need to be covered appropriately and men preferably trousers however my husband just wore a sarong over shorts. shoulders are also covered accordingly. make sure you take time to see the ancient paintings portraying the story of the relic and see the taxidermy elephant!

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text_clean: we were staying close to kandy and knew that this was one of the biggest attractions in the area and our only available day to go was on a saturday. we left early and got to the temple area around 930am. you must leave your shoes with a shoe keeper and buy your ticket in the same area. make sure you are properly dressed as they will not let you in with any knee or shoulder showing although you can buy a sarong right there if necessary. women and men go through separate security lines and for us, the lines were extremely long and quite slow-i believe this was because of our timing. from there, you can make your way into the main temple and line up in a hectic, crowded, and sweaty manner for a very quick look at the golden casket which holds the sacred tooth of buddha. from there, you are free to wander the grounds and look into the different buildings, including a museum with artifacts under glass, a room devoted to the famous temple elephant raja the tusker, and also some archeological artifacts. altogether a very fascinating look into the passionate devotion to buddha in sri lanka.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text_clean: we visited this temple as part of an organised tour with walkers tours and definitely benefited from having our guide, sumith, giving his insight and sharing his expertise whilst we were there. i dont think the experience would have been the same without this personal insight and informed commentary. firstly, to be clear you do not see the sacred tooth! if you are lucky you may get a quick peek at the casket with its separate 5 locks where it is housed. if you are a tourist you can reach this by one very quick queue where buddhists who wish to leave an offering may queue for 3 hours to reach the relic. the feeling of reference and respect is overwhelming and moving, just close your eyes for a moment and take in the sounds of chanting and drumming, the smells of essence and offerings, the emotions shown by people of faith. i can honestly say i felt completely overcome and still shiver at the memory. on leaving this area there is plenty more to see which are less crowded and easier to view. we particularly enjoyed the room with the pictures outlining the history of the sacred tooth around a statue of buddha with another place for offerings a must do place in kandy, particularly if you can have an insight as to why it is so important to the people of sri lanka
aspect_sentences: ['the feeling of reference and respect is overwhelming and moving, just close your eyes for a moment and take in the sounds of chanting and drumming, the smells of essence and offerings, the emotions shown by people of faith.']

review_text_clean: we visited this temple as part of an organised tour with walkers tours and definitely benefited from having our guide, sumith, giving his insight and sharing his expertise whilst we were there. i dont think the experience would have been the same without this personal insight and informed commentary. firstly, to be clear you do not see the sacred tooth! if you are lucky you may get a quick peek at the casket with its separate 5 locks where it is housed. if you are a tourist you can reach this by one very quick queue where buddhists who wish to leave an offering may queue for 3 hours to reach the relic. the feeling of reference and respect is overwhelming and moving, just close your eyes for a moment and take in the sounds of chanting and drumming, the smells of essence and offerings, the emotions shown by people of faith. i can honestly say i felt completely overcome and still shiver at the memory. on leaving this area there is plenty more to see which are less crowded and easier to view. we particularly enjoyed the room with the pictures outlining the history of the sacred tooth around a statue of buddha with another place for offerings a must do place in kandy, particularly if you can have an insight as to why it is so important to the people of sri lanka

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text_clean: temple of the sacred tooth relic is a buddhist temple in the city of kandy, sri lanka. it is located in the royal palace complex of the former kingdom of kandy. it is a very important sri lankan temple as it houses the relic of the tooth of the buddha. we visited this temple as part of a g adventures tour in the evening when the doors of the area where the casket that houses the tooth relic is open, this allows the locals as well as the tourists to see this casket. due to problems with possible terrorists, there are high security measures taken before you can enter the temple. you must also be appropriately dressed with women wearing clothes that cover their shoulders and knees and men should wear full length pants. most of the locals wear complete white outfits to show their respect when visiting the temple. it is a very busy in this temple and you cannot wear your shoes in it. i had a guide help me through the temple, which i would not have been able to do if he had not helped me up and down the numerous stairs you need to use to see the entire temple. the museum that is attached to the temple was also interesting to see as it held many sacred texts about buddhas life.
aspect_sentences: ['temple of the sacred tooth relic is a buddhist temple in the city of kandy, sri lanka.']

review_text_clean: this cave temple is one of the best preserved rock edifices and the caves have numerous statues and paintings, on the walls and roofs. there is a lot of history attached to this place. there are about 400 steps to climb up to the temple and can be reasonably managed by most age groups. you can either come down the same way or on the opposite side, that comes out at the golden temple.
aspect_sentences: ['there is a lot of history attached to this place.']

review_text_clean: from the car park, there is a 10-minute walk upstairs, it is steep but mostly in the shade. the caves are next to each other and the total time you need for this place is about 1 hour. the cave temples are well preserved and very richly decorated -statues, wall and ceiling paintings with vivid colours and nice details. absolutely worth visiting. after looking at other drip-ledge caves this brings the whole idea to a new level. some caves are lit up by nice yellow lights, which are properly positioned and i assume to give some resemblance to the candles once used in those temples. others, unfortunately, are blasted in all directions by bright white hospital-like lights. on our way out we decided to revisit some caves, but the power was down, so if you are unlucky to visit during a power outage you wont be able to fully enjoy this site. entrance fee 1500 lkr guide sign says 750, the one who tried to trick us into guiding us offered his services at 500 before us declining his offers, unfortunately, i couldnt understand him well. some unpleasant things - we encountered a very rude staff member at the entrance. - scaffolding has been left inside some of the caves, despite no signs of any work going on. ruins the atmosphere and some photos. - no information at the site at all, hire a guide or read online.
aspect_sentences: ['entrance fee 1500 lkr guide sign says 750, the one who tried to trick us into guiding us offered his services at 500 before us declining his offers, unfortunately, i couldnt understand him well.', 'some unpleasant things - we encountered a very rude staff member at the entrance.']

review_text_clean: this is a really interesting place. its a small temple complex at the top of a hill off of the main road through dambulla town. it is quite a long, steep climb from the golden buddha statue up the steps to the caves so take your time. no shoes allowed in the temple area theres a place to store them outside the entrance so have some socks with you as it is very hot underfoot. once youre in, there are five main caves accessed by a small temple facade built into the rock face. in each of the caves there are lots of buddha statues of various sizes ranging from human sized up to massive lying down buddhas about 15 metres long. take a note of the ornately painted cave ceilings too. depending on when you visit, the monks do occasionally shut the caves for prayer, but no problem its only for about 15 minutes. tip - if youre driving or being driven, enter by the rear steps on the access road a little further into town, as this way you pass the ticket office. otherwise youll climb all the way up to the entrance and then have to descend by about 100 steps down to buy your ticket, then climb back up again to get in.

review_text_clean: this site is also known as the golden temple of dambulla, a unesco site, and the largest and best-preserved cave temple complex in sri lanka. the climb to the caves can be fairly taxing depending on age and fitness levels, but worth the effort to view this great complex. there are five caves containing in excess of 150 statues, and extensive murals relating to the gautama buddha and his life. the caves are formed by a very large overhang in the face of the rock that has been partitioned and now sits behind a structure of white painted arched colonnades and gabled entrances. it is a mystical site. enjoy wonderful panoramic views outside, the sun shone and the rock of sigiriya was visible in the distance. the visit was made more relevant and informative by our excellent tour guide.

review_text_clean: there is a flight of stairs before reaching the temple. the route has shade. there are many monkeys so make sure not to feed them and keep your bags closed and belongings in check so the monkeys will cannot snatch them. we entered the temple complex on foot. when visiting any of the temples in sri lanka, it is a must that the knees and shoulders are always covered. wear modest clothes during your trip. bring along a skirt and a shawl inside your bag. it really comes in handy. as i entered each of the five chambers of the golden temple, i felt a sense of serenity thats almost overwhelming. when planning your trip to sri lanka, dont miss this temple. it is amazing, i guarantee. take some time to close your eyes and meditate for a few minutes. dambulla royal cave temple or the golden cave temple of dambulla is the most well preserved cave temple in sri lanka. the paintings and statues depict the life of gautama buddha. the paintings on the walls and the ceilings tell many stories. these paintings are all made from natural dyes mainly from saps of plants.

review_text_clean: it was early evening when we arrived at the temple of five caves of varying size and interior dated 1st bc. there are more than 80 caves in the area with the 5 caves most worth viewing. the first king turned the caves into a temple complex and many kings added to it later until the 11th century. it is still a functioning temple complex till this day. the spectacular murals on the ceilings were of sheer magnificence. they depicted buddhas life and sermons. the guide pointed out the large statue of the reclining buddha on his deathbed judging by the way the feet was displayed. stupas, a hundred small buddha statues, some gods and goddesses and kings statues were on display. one of the five caves was under repair, and we managed to take a quick look of it. the second cave was the largest and most impressive. they say you must never turn your back to the buddha when taking a photo. i felt intense spiritual power in these ancient caves and decided against taking any pictures out of respect. there was a small basin with water dripping down from the ceiling that the guide said would never dry up and have healing powers. once out of the temple caves we realised how the temple was cut out of a massive overhanging rock. we went under a huge bodhi tree and made a wish. it was just too bad we could not find time to see the ancient bodhi tree at anuradhapura. a very moving spiritual experience indeed.
aspect_sentences: ['the guide pointed out the large statue of the reclining buddha on his deathbed judging by the way the feet was displayed.']

review_text_clean: the climb up the steps to the temple offers some wonderful views including a panorama of lion rock and pidurangala rock. it is steep in places, so take some water with you theres nowhere to buy any at the top! you need to leave your shoes 100 rps per person and entry to the temple complex is 1500 rps each. remember to dress appropriately for visiting a temple. there are 5 caves the newest being the furthest away. perhaps worth starting here and working back as the older caves have the better workmanship. the statues and wall paintings are very impressive. you can get up close which is maybe not such a good thing given the age of some of the caves. there is little or no information whilst walking around. if you are touring sri lanka with a guide, then not a problem as the guide will relay the important information. otherwise read up beforehand as part of what makes it really impressive is the knowledge that some parts are over 2000 years old! the whole visit only takes an hour or so. for us it was a really convenient stopping off point on the drive between kandy and habarana where we based ourselves to see lion rock, minneriya and polonnaruwa

review_text_clean: the dambulla cave temple is reached by climbing a lot of steps. the trick is to make sure you buy your ticket to enter the caves at the bottom of the steps, as it is not obvious this is the process. to enter most buddhist temples you need to dress modestly, no exposed shoulders and knees covered - they do rent items to cover you at the temple entrance. you also need to pay to have your shoes minded whilst you are in the temple and the person you pay is very reluctant to give change so make sure you have the exact amount of 25 rupees. the cost to enter the cave is 1500 rupees. there are five caves and they are stocked with many buddhas in all manner of positions - if you are yet to visit myanmar, thailand, or other such buddhist countries you will be amazed, but to be honest the south east asian countries have many of these caves and do it all a lot better. it is though an interesting experience to visit this cave temple.

review_text_clean: you dont need a guide, just a guide book to appreciate the history and beauty of the cave temples. you will need to wear clothes that cover your knees and your shoulders. dont be one of those disrespectful tourists that hasnt bothered and has to borrow a sarong. also, its worth wearing socks - you are asked to take your shoes off but the rock paving is very hot by the afternoon and hard to walk on in bare feet - socks help! the temples date back to the 1st century bc and there is evidence of settlement here before that. the main attractions are 5 caves full of ancient buddhist frescos and buddha statues. because they have been protected from sunlight the colours are vivid and beautiful. the whole place is very peaceful and relaxing - enjoy. also, there are lots of monkeys outside who provide great entertainment!

review_text_clean: there are two paths up to the caves. one has steps the other a steep slope. we didnt fancy the steps so went the other way, which i believe takes a bit longer. it was a bit of a trek, but fine, definitely worth it to see the cave temple. its amazing how tranquil they are considering the crowds. there are 5 caves in all. the first one is tiny so some patience and queuing is needed. the second one is huge and the third is pretty big too. when youve seen those three youve seen the best of it and the other caves are just more of the same. remember to cover your shoulders and knees. take a pair of socks because you cant wear shoes inside. they will look after your shoes outside the entrance for 50sr a pair. otherwise take a bag and carry them around. also, most importantly dont pose for pictures with your back to budda, its a big no no. the path to the left on the way down leads you to the golden temple of dambulla, with its giant budda, which is worth seeing just by itself. overall this was definitely worth the trek and were happy we saw this impressive cave temple. iain, london

review_text_clean: stopped here on our tour of sri lankas cultural triangle. very interesting place and worth a visit and worth climbing all the steps. a few pointers its worth having a guide with you. we were on a private tour of the country with a driverguide and he was able to explain the history of the caves and the significance of the paintings in each one. it would have been quite difficult to have the same appreciation if you just went up and looked around by yourself. its a fully functioning religious site, of huge significance to the sri lankan people. there are periods of worship throughout the day when visitors need to wait outside. both ladies and gentlemen need to wear clothes which cover the elbows and their knees. transgressors were turned away without exception and left at the mercy of the very enterprising sarong salesman on the steps outside! our guide intervened when a japanese tourist was about to commit the massively disrespectful offence of photographing his companion with her back to an image of buddha. there are warnings about this everywhere and in every guide book, so there is really no excuse.

review_text_clean: the dumbulla rock temple is an impressive and interesting place to visit. however, be warned that there are approximately 350 steps to navigate before you reach the actual caves! i would definitely recommend going during the early part of the morning, before the heat starts to rise. as you enter the complex, you are greeted by a magnificent buddha statue, and a general information center. then the ascent begins. i am fairly fit, and it took me and our group about 40 minutes to get to the caves, with a few rest bite stops. please remember to wear clothes which are longer than knee length as you will not be able to enter. they only seem to charge foreigners approximately 7, to enter the main cave complex, which i dont think is fair, as either everyone should pay something, or it should be free for all. either way, the caves are impressive, with several ancient paintings and statues, created over several centuries by devotees to lord buddha. as we all religious sites, it is always an interesting visit, and the history of the caves are impressive. as an added bonus, the views from the top are breathtaking and shows the real beauty of sri lanka. definitely worth a visit, but go early to avoid the crowds and the heat.

review_text_clean: the walk up is scenic and the steps manageable as you can admire the view and take photos if you need a breather. go early because its cooler and especially at the weekend when the locals will visit to pray. its the largest conserved cave temple in sri lanka. there are four caves containing statues and painted images of budda. the paintings cover the walls and ceilings and you need to allow your eyes to acclimatise to the dim lighting and then take in the detail. it was pretty busy on the sunday morning that we visited and the caves were humid and full of visitors trying to get the perfect shot which created some bottle necks. then, in the midst of all the tourist footfall, there were the local worshippers making their offerings which helped to remind you what this place is really all about. its worth taking some quiet time to soak up the atmosphere and to enjoy the place before heading back down. dress modestly, remove your shoes and turn off the flash.

review_text_clean: having been to a large number of buddist temple sites in se asia - including other cave temples - i found dambulla interesting and beautiful but not entirely unique. if you have not been to many other places that are similar it is definitely a must visit. otherwise, id recommend it if you have time and interest in this type of attraction but i would not rearrange my schedule to fit it in. the caves themselves are not very large and are quite warm inside. the walls and ceilings are painted and beautiful to look at - more so then the buddhas in my opinion. the lighting is rough for photography unless you have specialized equipment. the caves are dark with spotlights in various areas. this makes the location less of an instagram-worthy location if thats your thing but most people should enjoy the sights just fine. id recommend going first thing in the morning to avoid crowds and to avoid the heat. the caves were already hot at 8 am so i cant imagine what it gets like later in the day. also be prepared to climb stairs to get there. about 365 of them. its steep and while i thought it was worth the cardio workout - someone who is out of shape or who has impaired mobility may not be able to make it. tips - dont forget to wear long pants and tops with shoulders covered. men included. or bring a sarong to wrap around if you have shorts on. - this is a buddhist temple so you need to leave your shoes near the entrance there is a safe location to do so and walk around barefoot. you will be walking on stoneconcrete. - with the climb up and plenty of time spent in each cave we did the whole thing in 1.5 hours. - there is plenty of parking and clean bathrooms at the bottom of the stairs for public use.
aspect_sentences: ['id recommend going first thing in the morning to avoid crowds and to avoid the heat.']

review_text_clean: we visited the dambulla caves on the 18th of december 2018. the caves are at a slight altitude so i would recommend wearing something comfortable for a 20-30 minute hike up some steep steps. also there were many monkeys near the steps so i would recommend not taking anything edible like fruits etc openly since it could attract the monkeys. also remember that there is an entrance fee of 1500 lkr so dont forget to buy these tickets before climbing the steps once you climb the steps and reach the top, the view is absolutely beautiful! there is a place to store your footwear near the cave complex just besides the entrance. the caves themselves are very beautiful and i would recommend that you take your best nightlow light photography equipment you have. the paintings on the top of the caves are very colorful and detailed and you would definitely want to take a few shots of these pictures. the statues of the buddhas in various poses are a real sight to see. the cave complex itself is very well maintained and shouldnt take you more than 50-60 minutes to complete. tip if you plan to visit the temple complex during the evening i would highly recommend a torch light and some mosquito repellent. it can get very dark once the sun sets and there were many mosquitos on the way down mainly because of the surrounding forests. this place is definitely worth a visit with family and friends.
aspect_sentences: ['the cave complex itself is very well maintained and shouldnt take you more than 50-60 minutes to complete.']

review_text_clean: its a steep climb up well made steps to reach the caves which are actually rock overhangs which have walls to protect them from the elements. this is is also the site of a monastery and at times of worship preceded by drumming the caves are closed to the public for a short time. its a temple and ladies must have legs and shoulders covered, no shorts or vest tops for men. shoes are left at the top of the steps take socks in hot weather so you dont burn your feet in the courtyard. the art on the walls and ceilings is magnificent at times looking like beautiful embroidery. the lighting makes the caves very atmospheric with the numerous buddha statues illuminated. its well worth reading up on the caves before you visit as they all date from different periods. the far left cave has had some poor restoration ... it would have been better to leave it as it was. you can buy lotus flowers by the main road to leave as offerings. it is a wonderful place of great beauty.

review_text_clean: be prepared for a long, steep climb following the kings way! but worth it and the inevitable stops allow the admire the stunning views over the country side. as in some other places of worship, shoes have to be taken off. may be wearing socks is a good idea. engaging a guide is highly recommended. ours was really very good and gave us information broader than only concerning the temple. the temple in the five caves starts from 100 bc - caves 1,2 and 4. the fifth cave is from the beginning of xx century. there are impressive statures of the buddha as well as other statues all from different materials. the wall frescoes are from later times or have been repainted later. really interesting and impressive. there is a stupa which appears broken and repaired. and indeed it had been broken in 1936 and all the treasures, jewellery donated by kings and queens through time, have been stolen. regrettably, never found and recovered. highly recommended and it is a must as it sheds light on sri lankan history and relation to buddhism, stimulating further learning about this nation.

review_text_clean: the dambulla cave temple, also known as the golden temple of dambulla, is a must-visit attraction when traveling to sri lanka. located just 10 minutes away from dambulla village, the temple can be easily reached by bus or tuk-tuk. the entrance fee is 2000 lkr around 5 euros, which is well worth the cost to experience this unique and sacred place. upon arrival, visitors must remove their shoes and dress appropriately out of respect for the temple. the climb to reach the temple takes around 20 minutes, but the views of the surrounding mountains along the way are breathtaking and make the journey even more worthwhile. the dambulla temple is divided into two parts the temple cave and the golden buddha. its important to note that if you want to see the golden buddha, you should not go back to the main entrance. instead, continue on to the lower level of the temple, where the golden buddha is located. inside the temple cave, visitors will be amazed by the intricate and well-preserved ancient cave paintings and statues of the buddha. the peaceful atmosphere of the temple is truly awe-inspiring, and visitors can take their time to explore the cave and take in the stunning surroundings. overall, the dambulla cave temple is an unforgettable experience that shouldnt be missed when visiting sri lanka. the climb to the temple may be a bit challenging, but the reward of exploring this sacred and historical site, along with the breathtaking views of the mountains, is worth the effort.

review_text_clean: visited the cave complex from habarana for a few hours after a day by the pool. easy to get to by bus 4548 from habarana junction in direction of kandy but make sure they let you off by the front of the golden buddha rather than in town my conductor refused for some reason which meant a bit of a long walk. as others have said i can highly recommend getting a tuk tuk round to the ticket office then its only a short climb up to the top 15 mins. once you are up there the views are epic, if you go late afternoon around 4.30pm for me there are not too many people around so easier to see the caves properly. suggesting starting from the furthest cave and working your way back towards the entrance as this gives you more of a build up. caves were impressive and had a really peaceful atmosphere, highly recommended. afterwards just head down main staircase and flag down a bus going back your direction from the road.

review_text_clean: as this is a temple be prepared to dress appropriately, knees and shoulders covered for both men and women. note that unlike some temples around the world there is no option outside the temple to hire a sarong type thing to cover up with. plan your day accordingly and do what we did, which was to do a quick change in to long pants inside our van prior to heading to the temple, our last activity for the day. we had a guide which was organised by our driver, he was very good sharing extensive knowledge throughout the various caves. be mindful when taking photos as it is disrespectful to face your back to buddha, so dont try and take selfies with buddha in the background. you need to leave your shoes outside with attendants who charge you a small donation fee, you pay the fee on retrieval of your shoes so have some small change on you. the caves are amazing and will take approx an hour at the most depending on how much your guide likes to talk to complete the caves. another must see while in sri lanka.

review_text_clean: the caves at dambulla blew us away! we very nearly missed them as we didnt wish to stay in dambulla. however we figured we would give it a try and see what might happen. well it seems like we arent the only back packers not wishing to spend a night there and a couple of guys have caught on to the trend and have made themselves a great little business. it goes like this you get off the bus in dambulla, catch a tuk tuk to the caves where you find a really nice helpful guy willing to look after your back pack in his shed for free! well we believed him as did a number of others off we went up the stairs without the additional weight of our back packs, all 320... it was truly one of the best sights in srilanka! on our return we picked up our bags, a donation was suggested, some paid some didnt. however these guys knew we didnt plan to stay so this is when the real business kicked in, bartering a price for a tuk tuk to our next destination. we went onwards to sigiriya others to kandy the price agreed in was fair and all in all it worked out perfectly so pleased we made the effort and tried our luck

review_text_clean: dambulla cave temple alsop known as the golden temple of dambulla is a world heritage site 1991 in sri lanka, situated in the central part of the country. dambulla is the largest and best-preserved cave temple complex in sri lanka. the rock towers 160 m over the surrounding plains. there are more than 80 documented caves in the surrounding area. major attractions are spread over five caves, which contain statues and paintings. these paintings and statues are related to gautama buddha and his life. there are a total of 153 buddha statues, three statues of sri lankan kings and four statues of gods and goddesses. the latter include vishnu and the ganesha. the murals cover an area of 2,100 square metres 23,000 sq ft. depictions on the walls of the caves include the temptation by the demon mara, and buddhas first sermon. the dambulla cave monastery is still functional and remains the best-preserved ancient edifice in sri lanka. source wikipedia it is a must visit as the statues and paintings are such a delight to the eye. the serenity of the place is something not to be missed. its not a tough climb and can be completed in about 15 mins up and down. we were blessed with light showers which made the climb bit risky, it was indeed worth the effort.

review_text_clean: we made a short visit to this cave temple on way to sigiriya. it was historic and magnificent and is still used as place of worship. entrance fee for adult is lkr1,500- each. as it was a religious public holiday, we saw many worshippers too and walked up to the temple with one family who showed us the way. i tried to walk barefoot with them but was too much for me. they told me it was okay to wear my shoes up and took it off before entering the temple. we left our shoes at the shoes counter for lkr25- a pair, no tickets are issued for this but the man with fuzzy hair assured us not to worry as he would remember whose shoes they belong to. alternatively, you can leave your shoes in the open at your own risk. there are many buddha statues in the various caves, a bit dark inside the caves but interesting sights to see how this worship place for many centuries are within the caves.

review_text_clean: a short hike up the hill, the dambulla cave temples are a really great place to be. as it is a working temple, you need to be covered shoulders and below the knees, and take off your shoes when you get there, but this is normal practice around sri lanka. the 5 temples are cut into the side of the rock - put there by different kings across time, to show their devotion to buddhism. do beware of the guides that will talk you through the first cave and then offer to take you around the others in return for payment - you can just say no and they will leave you alone. they are beautiful, the detail and differences between them is amazing. there is also a bag drop in the buddhist book centre at the bottom of the hill so if you come with travelling backpacks you can leave them there!

review_text_clean: the dambulla cave temple, famous for its ancient mural paintings depicting the life and work of buddha, is a significant site for cultural and history of sri lanka. there are five caves housing statuses of buddha from different time ranging from 1 century bc to some 200 years ago. its advisable to get some background of it or hire a guide in white clothes from the temple to walk you through. there are so much subtleties on display - for examples, the different postures of buddha, the material used at different era and the reasons. there are 2 ways of reaching the temple - one from the golden temple from town, and the other one from an open car park. the latter one is shorter but the view is breath taking.

review_text_clean: if you have travelled much around south-east asia you will have seen all of this before, often better and probably for free. sure, the setting is a novelty with the temples set inside five decorated caves and there are an incredible number of buddha statues but, fundamentally, there is little to set the place apart. we had anticipated a series of caverns but the caves are actually 5 individual units. inside each the lighting is subdued and, as a result, the whole atmosphere is gloomy and uninspiring. we have visited many, many temples in the likes of thailand, myanmar and cambodia, generally without charge, and seen some stunning interiors. sadly this place didnt live up to those standards. on a practical level, the ticket office is located a considerable distance from the road which makes for a significant walk for those arriving independently before you even begin the climb up the hill. enter at the golden temple, follow the sign for the cave temple and just keep going until, eventually, you get to the ticket office. at 1500 rupees we felt the entry charge was way too much for what is on offer. also, remember to take a sarong or else you will have to hire one there at additional charge including men if youre wearing shorts.
aspect_sentences: ['on a practical level, the ticket office is located a considerable distance from the road which makes for a significant walk for those arriving independently before you even begin the climb up the hill.']
